4410695e-1450-5263-a481-fa1c0e2e7a22.name: Khan al-Harir
4410695e-1450-5263-a481-fa1c0e2e7a22.description:
Khan al-Harir was constructed in AH 981 / AD 1573–4 by order of Darwish Pasha, the Governor of Damascus at the time. He founded it as a *waqf* to benefit the Darwishiyya Mosque. First called Qaysariyyat Darwish Basha, it was later renamed according to its function into Khan al-Harir, the silk *caravanserai*.  
The building is nearly square in plan, occupying around 2,500 sq m, and including 27 roofed shops embedded within its exterior walls. The central entrance on the northern wall gives access to an open courtyard of about 300 sq m, which is surrounded by two rows of chambers that originally accommodated the silk workshops and merchants. The courtyard is paved with black rectangular stones with a rectangular fountain in the centre. In line with the style of damascene *khan* in general, it has two floors. Stairs on each side behind the entrance portal lead up to an upper floor. There, the former accommodation rooms are laid out along both sides of a corridor, while on the east side there are rooms along the inner courtyard side only. All the chambers are either cross- or barrel-vaulted. Above the entrance there are three barrel-vaulted rooms; the one facing outwards was the chamber of the guard, while the chamber facing the courtyard was the room of the *khanji*, the *khan* supervisor. The building is roofed with a row of 44 cupolas above the corridor. Three sides of the *khan* face on to alleyways, characterised by alternating courses of polychrome masonry (*ablaq*), a typical feature of the Mamluk-Ottoman architecture in Damascus.  
The layout of Khan al-Harir, with its open central courtyard and water fountain, is exemplary of *caravanserais* throughout the Arab-Islamic world. It follows the traditional Ottoman principles of construction, including a large courtyard and galleries, topped with the typical small cupolas. It should, however, be taken into consideration that no Mamluk *khan*s have survived in Damascus to determine the Mamluk influence on these Ottoman commercial structures.  
In contrast to the *khan*s on the trade routes that initially served as resting and lodging places, the city *caravanserais* were wholesale centres. Khan al-Harir had several functions, combining accommodation, workshops and a trading post, a venue for the sale of goods produced at the *khan*, and the sale of raw materials used in the manufacturing processes practised there.  
Inspired by the high level of building activity of the Sultans, local notables, particularly the governors, expounded an active building programme before the end of the AH 10th / AD 16th century concentrated on two areas: mosques with affiliating structures were built to the west of the city, while the market was extended by the construction of a number of *khans* to the southwest of the Great Umayyad Mosque. The Khan al-Harir was the first great *caravanserai* inside the city walls. Its construction was the beginning of a shift in mercantile activity to the area southwest of the Umayyad Mosque.
4410695e-1450-5263-a481-fa1c0e2e7a22.short_description: This caravanserai was built as a *waqf* (endowment) by one of the early Ottoman governors of Damascus, Darwish Pasha, to benefit his mosque. Since it specialised in silk-trading it was later called the Khan al-Harir (Silk Caravanserai). It is a huge structure in the heart of the trading area south of the Umayyad Mosque, occupying around 2,500 sq m, including 27 roofed shops around a square courtyard. The chambers are cross-vaulted and domed by little cupolas in typical Ottoman style.
4410695e-1450-5263-a481-fa1c0e2e7a22.method_for_datation: The inscription above the entrance mentions both the patron and the year of construction.

44db66ac-94d1-513a-affd-eaec477e9022.name: Citadel of Amman (general view).
44db66ac-94d1-513a-affd-eaec477e9022.description:
Muslim troops led by Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan conquered Amman in AH 13 / AD 634. Under Umayyad rule, Amman was the capital city of al-Balqa district. A new residential and administrative complex (Dar al-Imara) was built on the Citadel of Amman. The site known in Arabic as al-Qal'a is a well-defined natural elevation at the heart of ancient and modern Amman. The Umayyad town at the citadel comprised a palace complex: a bath complex; a deep, round water reservoir; a central plaza, a congregational mosque and domestic quarters, all of which were enclosed within fortified walls.  
The proximity of the city to the centre of power in Damascus, together with the fact that the area was inhabited by tribes traditionally allied to the Umayyad dynasty, had created a favourable atmosphere for the economic development of al-Balqa in general, and Amman in particular. The city flourished during the Umayyad period benefiting from its strategic location on the trade and pilgrimage route between Damascus and Hijaz. Amman lost some of its political significance with the shift of the political centre of the Islamic state to Iraq and declined slightly during the Abbasid period (AH 132–358 / AD 750–969), and yet even more rapidly in the Fatimid period (AH 358–566 / AD 969–1171). By the AH 8th / AD 14th century, Amman was all but lost from historical memory. The Medieval Arab historian Abu al-Fida wrote of Amman in AH 720 / AD 1321: 'A very ancient town and was ruined before the days of Islam'.  
In AH 1296 / AD 1879 the Ottoman administration helped to settle emigrants from the Caucasus into a few areas in Jordan including Amman. In 1921 Amman became the capital city of the newly established Emirate of Transjordan founded by the Amir (later king) Abdullah I.  
  
Click [here](< https://youtu.be/yHVm_pbN70Q>) to **watch a video presentation** of this artefact.
44db66ac-94d1-513a-affd-eaec477e9022.short_description: The Citadel of Amman is a natural elevation within Amman. Muslim troops led by Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan conquered Amman in AH 13 / AD 634, and under Umayyad rule it was the capital of al-Balqa district. The Umayyad town at the citadel comprised a palace complex, a bath, a reservoir, a plaza, a congregational mosque and domestic quarters within fortified walls. The city flourished during the Umayyad period due to its proximity to Damascus but started to decline in the Abbasid period and was abandoned by the 8th / 14th century until 1296 / 1879 when the Ottomans settled Caucasian emigrants in Amman.

4637b883-3f04-595d-8275-01f5645225cb.name: La gare Midan, Damas (The Midan Station, Damascus)
4637b883-3f04-595d-8275-01f5645225cb.description: The Midan Station is located south of Damascus in Al Midan neighbourhood. It predates both the Qadam and Qanawat stations and was the first railway station to be built in Damascus. The Midan Station was part of the region's earliest railway network owned by the French company Société des Chemins de fer Ottomans Économiques de Beyrouth-Damas-Hauran en Syrie, later known as Damas-Hama et Prolongements (D.H.P.). The company's first railway, the Hauran Railway (Damascus–Muzairib), opened in 1894. During the planning of the Hijaz Railway, unsuccessful attempts were made to purchase the Hauran Railway. As a result, a parallel railway line was constructed, and both lines remained in operation until the First World War, when foreign-owned railways belonging to companies based in enemy territory were confiscated. This included the Hauran Railway, whose operation was subsequently transferred to the Hijaz Railway.

4904fdee-4fc9-5975-9b59-b15c67487eee.name: Deraa : the railway junction between the Palestine system and the Mecca-Hedjaz Railway
4904fdee-4fc9-5975-9b59-b15c67487eee.description: This painting of Donald Maxwell of Deraa depicts a camel caravan crossing an open landscape, with buildings and walls in the distance. Deraa formed the junction between two railway lines: the main Hijaz Railway connecting Damascus to Medina, and the branch extending westwards to the Mediterranean port of Haifa. Situated in the Hauran plain, 123 kilometers by rail from Damascus, the station connected the north-south route with the coast. This link enabled construction materials and equipment arriving at Haifa to reach the Hijaz Railway, while agricultural produce from Deraa and the Syrian interior could travel in the opposite direction for exports to European markets. The railway stimulated economic activity in Deraa and its surroundings, strengthening the town’s role as a center connecting the agricultural hinterland with maritime trade.

4ab16da1-9584-56f4-a5d1-9e9d260e8256.name: The Arab Train Song
4ab16da1-9584-56f4-a5d1-9e9d260e8256.description: The Arab Train (Ughniyat al-Qitar al-Arabi), a children’s song performed by the Syrian singer and composer Mohammed Diya Al-Din (1932–1978), survives in a black-and-white recording from the archive of Jordanian Television dated 1972. Addressing the driver of an imaginary “Arab train”, the singer asks to be taken to his loved ones in Egypt, Syria and Libya, sends greetings to Kuwait, Qatar, Abu Dhabi and his brothers in Saudi Arabia, several of them newly independent states at the time, wishes to visit Lebanon and his family in Jordan and Iraq, and asks the driver to pass through Sudan and Morocco and stop in Bahrain. With its playful refrain imitating the sound of a train, the song turns the idea of Arab unity into a journey for children, in which borders and distances disappear and the only worry is missing the train. It shows how the railway, long after the Hijaz Railway had ceased to function as a continuous line, lived on in popular culture as an image of connection.

4c6c73fd-b2b8-5169-9f5b-defe03f3bbce.name: *Bilder aus Mekka von C. Snouck Hurgronje*, published Leiden, 1889
4c6c73fd-b2b8-5169-9f5b-defe03f3bbce.short_description:
*Bilder aus Mekka* was published in 1889 by the Dutch orientalist Christiaan Snouck Hurgronje. Consisting of 20 collotype prints mounted on 18 leaves, it is one of the earliest photographic records of the Hajj, preceded only by photographs taken in 1881 by Muhammed Sadiq Bey. *Bilder aus Mekka*came one year after *Bilder-Atlas zu Mekka*. This was a collection of lithographs including images predominantly of Mecca and portraits of pilgrims, taken by Snouck himself on his research trip to Jidda and Mecca between August 1884–August 1885. Alongside this he published *Mekka*a work that focussed on the history of Mecca and the origins of Islam. Following on from the publication of these two volumes, and having not been able to photograph the hajj himself, Snouck used images taken by a Meccan physician named ‘Abd al-Ghaffar of the Hajj of August 1888 to publish *Bilder aus Mekka*.  
Snouck met ‘Abd al-Ghaffar during his stay in Mecca in 1885, and although ‘Abd al-Ghaffar was already familiar with photography, Snouck is supposed to have helped refine his skills and he became Snouck’s photographic assistant during the six months he was in Mecca.  
The photographs include views of Mecca, Mina and Arafat, and depict the various stages of Hajj. Although traces of ‘Abd al-Ghaffar’s signature are still visible on the photographs, there is clear evidence of an attempt to erase them by Snouck. A summary text written by Snouck opens the volume and a list of plates precedes the images.

The report is incomplete; 11 pages are related to Iraq (pp. 54-85), while 16 pages cover Iran (pp. 73-160). The typewritten text is accompanied by photomechanical prints and technical drawings of locomotives. The report might have been produced both by the British or the American intelligence. It includes The Second World War-era British military map showing regional railway networks (established or under construction) in the (ex) Ottoman Empire. Manuscript annotations highlight the geopolitical interests of various nations involved in their construction. The piece also has the stamp of the Survey Directorate, GHQ Middle East.

54310c6d-87ca-585e-b552-bcb1c5951fe3.name: Dress
54310c6d-87ca-585e-b552-bcb1c5951fe3.short_description: This dress of al-Druze (Druse) women is made of a long grey with green and silver brocade, pursed narrow sleeves, wide, open square shaped chest, pursed at the middle and wide at the bottom with ruffles and a cotton liner. This object illustrates the variegated social composition and demographic changes in the Jordanian territory in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The al-Druze tribes migrated from Syria (Hawran) to north east Jordan in the early twentieth century because of their support for the Syrian revolution against the French occupation. The traditional Druse and other Jordanian costumes were influenced by the local trade and economic activities: as illustrated in this case, they were often made of silk textiles, produced in Syria and traded to Jordan and Palestine.

547b1024-4367-52b2-8fb3-a58228f14a14.name: La Gare de Hidjaz, Damas (The Hijaz Station, Damascus)
547b1024-4367-52b2-8fb3-a58228f14a14.description: The Hijaz Railway Station was designed by the Spanish architect Fernando de Aranda (1878–1969). Raised at the Ottoman court in Istanbul, where his father directed the Imperial Military Band, Aranda settled permanently in Damascus following the deposition of Sultan Abdülhamid II in 1909. The station was designed within the broader Hijaz Railway project directed by Heinrich August Meissner Pasha (1862–1940), the German civil engineer and Chief Engineer of the Hijaz Railway. Although Aranda never obtained formal architectural qualifications and could not officially sign his projects, he became one of Damascus's most influential architects, designing the Hijaz Railway Station alongside numerous public and private buildings that shaped the city's early twentieth-century urban landscape.

54f861aa-1d28-5c1b-b3c3-07e65ff10862.name: 'Picture of the Tents of the Turks'. Photographer: H. A. Mirza & Sons
54f861aa-1d28-5c1b-b3c3-07e65ff10862.description:
This image shows the tents of the Ottoman Turkish troops at their camp at Medina. Despite the apparently secular nature of the subject, and the fact that the camp does not depict a stopping-off point on the hadj, the laudatory poetry and prose makes clear the relevance of the image to the experience of the hadj – that is, that the Turks, as ‘military people of the highest rank’ serve Islam by defending and enabling the passage to Mecca and Medina for other Muslims.  
  
As with the other photographs in this album (Photo 174/1-13), whose subjects are architectural and landscape, the figures are not the subject of the image. However, a detailed examination of the image shows the soldiers going about their day-to-day activities, such as cooking and eating. The method by which the ground would have been prepared before a tent was erected is indicated by the empty low circular foundation in the lower left corner of the image. In the distance, in the right-hand background of the image, beyond the dry-stone wall delineating the camp, palm groves and permanent dwellings can be identified.

keywords: Travel; Hijaz; Medina; Mecca
materials: Mottled blue-tinted window mount, card, gelatin silver print, indigo ink (printed), red ink (hand-painted)

550798b2-2ff6-5c87-b3f5-df183a1a2b89.name: Bridal cushions (background: Maan section of Hijaz Railroad, Jordan)
550798b2-2ff6-5c87-b3f5-df183a1a2b89.description: Bridal cushions from Ma’an, Jordan, traditionally prepared by a bride as part of her trousseau for her new home, are among the most distinctive examples of Jordanian domestic textiles. Their fabrics and techniques reflect connections with textile traditions from the Caucasus, Syria, Turkey, and Central Asia, shaped through centuries of travel, trade, pilgrimage, and cultural exchange. These influences reached Ma’an through its position as an important crossroads on regional routes, particularly as a key stop along the Hijaz Railway, built during the Ottoman period to facilitate travel between Damascus and the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. The background image is from the G. Eric and Edith Matson Photograph Collection at the Library of Congress, showing the Hijaz Railway, which connected communities across the Ottoman Empire and facilitated movement for travellers, pilgrims, and merchants between the Levant and the Hijaz.

5529115f-b39d-54b6-8097-94b322f39015.name: Map of the Ottoman province (vilayet) of Beirut with its fife subdivisions (sancak).
5529115f-b39d-54b6-8097-94b322f39015.description: Vilayet of Beirut was established in 1888 as a separate Ottoman province as it extended along the eastern Mediterranean coast. The map key defines the five sanjaks within the vilayet: Beirut, Tripoli, Latakia, Acre and Nablus. The province incorporated territories now located between several modern states: Lebanon, Syria and Palestine. Railway routes are marked in red lines across the map. The line linking Beirut eastward across Mount Lebanon with Damascus represents the Beirut–Damascus railway, a 147-km line connecting the Mediterranean and the Syrian interior, crossing the mountainous terrain. It was opened in 1895 and operated by the Damas-Hama et Prolongements (D.H.P.) network.

559330fc-4f61-535a-9310-1782a48a785a.name: The Tell Clock Tower
559330fc-4f61-535a-9310-1782a48a785a.description: This clock tower is located in Al-Tell square, next to Al-Manshiyya, one of the oldest parks in Tripoli. The tower is 30 metres tall and consists of five separate floors.
559330fc-4f61-535a-9310-1782a48a785a.history: This clock tower was gifted to the city of Tripoli - like many clock towers of the Ottoman Empire, such as the famous Jaffa clock tower - and erected in 1906, to celebrate the 30th anniversary of Sultan 'Abd al-Hamid II's reign. The clock tower is now working again, following a full renovation in 1992, supported by personal funding from the honorary Turkish consul of Northern Lebanon, Sobhi Akkari.

564ae52d-7395-53f5-8794-d12cd20b98b5.name: Damas – La Grande Station du Hidjaz
564ae52d-7395-53f5-8794-d12cd20b98b5.description: The original northern terminus of the Hijaz Railway was Damascus Qadem Station, situated close to the old assembly point for the start of the traditional overland pilgrimage caravan. In 1911, however, it was decided to build a short three-kilometre extension to the centre of the city in order to provide a more prestigious front for the railway’s operations. Designed by the German architect, Palmer, in grand Ottoman style, Damascus Kanawat Station’s imposing lines and impressive interior befitted its position at the heart of the Syrian capital. Its central location also provided a more convenient departure point for both passenger and freight traffic. In a square close to the station, the official Hijaz Railway and Telegraph Monument was erected.

56672473-1926-594f-b790-6b908f455bae.name: Postcard published by Dimitri Tarazi & Fils. Beyrouth, Damas, Jérusalem (Postcard published by Dmimitri Tarazi and Sons, Beirut, Damascus, Jerusalem)
56672473-1926-594f-b790-6b908f455bae.description: The Mahmal al-Sharif and the Sanjak are the principal ceremonial symbols of the annual Syrian Hajj caravan departing from Damascus. The Mahmal was an elaborately embroidered ceremonial palanquin carried on a specially selected camel, and the Sanjak was the related banner. The tradition started during the Mamluk period and was later adopted by the Ottoman sultans as a symbol of their patronage of the pilgrimage and their role as Servants of the Two Holy Sanctuaries. A study by Behrens-Abouseif associated its origin with a legend related to the female Mamluk ruler, Shajarat al-Durr. The legend reflects the prominent participation of elite Mamluk women in pilgrimage and the exceptional political memory of Shajarat al-Durr as the first female ruler of the Mamluk Sultanate. For the people of Damascus, the Mahmal's departure and return were among the city's greatest religious and civic celebrations, drawing pilgrims, officials and large crowds into public processions that expressed communal participation in the Hajj.

56ae89a4-e69e-5467-915e-b99f5b5f752d.name: Panorama: al-hujjaj bi-mina yawn al-‘id al-akbar (‘The pilgrims at Mina on the day of the big feast’)
56ae89a4-e69e-5467-915e-b99f5b5f752d.description: Muhammad Sadiq Bey was the first person to take photographs of Mecca, Medina and the Hajj. An Egyptian army engineer and surveyor, he was also the treasurer of the Egyptian Hajj caravan, travelling numerous times to the Hijaz. Using a technique first invented in the 1850s, Sadiq Bey took his first photographs in 1861 using glass plate negatives, especially useful for large-format frames. His most important photographs, of both the buildings and interiors of the sanctuaries at Mecca and Medina, as well as sites at Arafat and Mina, were taken in 1861, 1880 and 1881. For the first time, the pilgrimage and the holy cities were precisely and realistically documented.

571615de-6d27-5fda-8d4c-3d97eedc3cc2.name: Grand Bazaar
571615de-6d27-5fda-8d4c-3d97eedc3cc2.description:
Known locally as the 'Covered Bazaar', the Grand Bazaar was the commercial heart of Istanbul during the Ottoman era. The bazaar centres around two *bedesten*s (a domed and guarded building where luxury goods such as silk and jewellery were stored and sold), namely the Inner and the Sandal *bedesten*s, built as *waqf*s (pious endowments) by Mehmed II soon after the Ottoman conquest of Istanbul. With time, the number *han*s (inns) and shops around them increased, and the bazaar evolved, through fires and earthquakes, into its present shape of a labyrinth of vaulted streets and alleys bordered by shops.  
The Inner Bedesten (also known as Cevahir or Old Bedesten) was built first. It is a rectangular masonry structure (45.30 x 29.50 m from the inside) with a gate in the middle of each of its sides. The interior is dominated by two rows of four thick piers connected by wide arches and supporting 15 domes, with the central dome reaching 14.89 m in height.  
The Sandal Bedesten (also known as the Small or New Bedesten) is name d after the cotton and silk textiles (sandal) sold there. It is somewhat smaller (40 m x 32 m from the inside) but is designed along the same general lines as the Inner Bedesten. It has three rows of four piers connected by wide arches and supporting 20 domes. Both structures are surrounded by attached shops from the outside, but remain physically prominent in relation to the rest of the bazaar.  
The bazaar currently has over 60 streets and about 4000 shops, including 14 *han*s, 2 *bedesten*s, as well as several mosques and fountains. The streets retain their old names, reflecting the old custom which gathered together artisans and/or shops producing or selling similar items. The Grand Bazaar has suffered considerable damage as a result of numerous fires since the 16th century, as well as earthquakes of 1766 and 1894, and has therefore undergone several periods of restoration work, the latest of which was completed in 1959. Today the Grand Bazaar is primarily a tourist attraction.  
Istanbul has three *bedesten*s, two as described above and a third, also built by Mehmed the Conqueror, is located in the Galata quarter. This is in contrast to other cities in the Ottoman Empire, which commonly had only one or two *bedesten*s, thus demonstrating the importance of the capital as a commercial centre.
571615de-6d27-5fda-8d4c-3d97eedc3cc2.short_description: The Grand Bazaar or Covered Bazaar of Istanbul developed around two *bedesten*s (guarded building for luxury goods) built by Mehmed II (the Conqueror) and is one of the most striking examples providing us with information on the commercial life of the Ottoman city. A gigantic commercial complex containing 2 *bedesten*s, 14 *han*s and about 4,000 shops, several *masjid*s and fountains, the Grand Bazaar has survived through great alterations and still serves as a bazaar.
571615de-6d27-5fda-8d4c-3d97eedc3cc2.dates: The two bedestens were built during the reign of Mehmed II ‘the Conqueror’, (his second reign AH 855–86 / AD 1451–81), and the bazaar developed around them.
571615de-6d27-5fda-8d4c-3d97eedc3cc2.method_for_datation: The monument can be dated based on endowment charters (*waqfiyya*) of Mehmed II, other various Ottoman archival documents, and contemporary accounts by travellers.

59c09c6e-e0cc-5963-83cc-fd6b4aea8244.name: Bakırköy Railway Station
59c09c6e-e0cc-5963-83cc-fd6b4aea8244.short_description: During the 19th century, new technologies radically transformed both travel and communications. The first railway in Anatolia was constructed between Izmir and Aydin. Ottoman railways were mainly built during the period of Abdülhamid II. The first railway in the Republic of Turkey was part of the İzmir-Aydın line, founded by a British company in 1860. The İzmir-Kasaba line was built in 1865, the Rumeli line in 1869-77, the Anatolia-Baghdad line in 1872 and the Mudanya-Bursa line in 1892.

59e106e1-b0a2-5505-af4e-7abfde04a90a.name: Belt
59e106e1-b0a2-5505-af4e-7abfde04a90a.short_description: Leather belt embellished with silver pieces decorated in niello with patterns and symbols at the end. Two silver rosette buckles at the end form a locking mechanism. This is an object produced by Circassian craftsmen. The immigration of the Circassians to the Ottoman Empire started in the middle of 19th century and continued until 1900. The Circassian communities migrated mostly to the eastern Arab countries, with which they had spiritual and religious links. They brought with them their traditional activities, crafts and decorative patterns. All these elements soon mingled with the local Arab society and became part of the social and economic landscape of the Arab countries.

5d117acd-215b-54b0-aefc-38ef0cc38d6b.name: Map of caravan routes
5d117acd-215b-54b0-aefc-38ef0cc38d6b.short_description: This map illustrates the trading caravan routes crossing the Sahara desert from Mediterranean ports (Tripoli, Tafilet, Tunis, Algiers and Oran) to sub-Saharan cities. The trading routes were connected north and south to three pilgrim routes for Mecca. The northern pilgrim route from Tunis and Tripoli included Siwah, Cairo, Suez and Aqaba. From Aqaba, meeting the pilgrim route from Damascus, it continued along the coast of Arabia to Mecca. The central route continued from Siwah through the oases of Dakkel and El-Kharjeh to ports on the Red Sea to Jeddah and Mecca. The southern route followed the valley of the Upper Niger through Timbuctu, Gao, Sokoto, Kano, Lake Chad and Kordofan to the port of Swakin on the Red Sea and continued to Jeddah by ship.
5d117acd-215b-54b0-aefc-38ef0cc38d6b.author: Maria Francesca Carvelli (MWNF)

5f2063c5-3816-5b41-a0c5-caa381690a87.name: Bosra Citadel
5f2063c5-3816-5b41-a0c5-caa381690a87.description:
As a major stronghold in the region and the palatial residence for the Ayyubid regent, the citadel became the focal point of the Islamic city. It was a Roman theatre transformed into a military structure by a series of constructions carried out during a period of more than 150 years. The initial period of alterations began under Gumushtagin in 481/1088, who built the two towers on top of the rectangular 9 m x 8 m stairwells flanking the scaena of the theatre, and consequently closed all the openings to the outside. Around 60 years later, the last Burid ruler of Damascus, Abu Sa‘id Abaq (534–49/1140–54), resumed the fortification extensions. He built the tower on the south-west façade of the cavea in 542/1147–8 in anticipation of a Crusader attack, as is evident from his epithet in the inscription: “qatil al-kafara wal-mushrikin”, “killer of the unbelievers and the polytheists”. These three towers from the first extension phase, covered in a simple and traditional way, have a flat roof of basalt-stone slabs supported by transverse arches.  
  
The second phase of fortification began with the Ayyubid ruler of Damascus, al-‘Adil Abu Bakr (r. 592–615/1196–1218). The towers, now erected at a considerable distance from the cavea proper, leave space for interior corridors and defence installations. Several antique structures from within the city must have been used for there is evidence of numerous spolia in this building phase. The additional towers, erected by al-‘Adil, are distinguished from earlier extensions by their considerably larger size, the construction technique of the outer walls and the barrel-vaulted roofs. The north-western tower measuring 22 m x 31 m was added in 599/1202–3, and was followed in 608–10/1211–13 by the two entrance towers. Passing these, the visitor finds himself in one of the defence alleyways around the theatre proper. Climbing the stairs one reaches the northern platform serving as an exhibition space for antique statues in front of tower. Together with tower, now accommodating the ethnographic collection, and tower that serves as archaeological museum, it belongs to the last, medieval, phase carried out to improve the citadel’s defences. All three towers are constructed in the splendid three-iwans mode, arranged around a central courtyard. Tower, since it is easy to reach from the entrance gate, might have served as a reception hall during the reign of al-Salih Isma‘il, who took up residence in the citadel.
5f2063c5-3816-5b41-a0c5-caa381690a87.author: Verena Daiber
keywords: Bosra; Bosra Citadel; Bosra Theatre; Ayyubid period

60125102-5ebb-5175-b8f6-33c1bd1dcafc.name: Le Port, Vue générale, Les Douanes et la Gare de D.H.P. Beyrouth (Syria) (The Port Overview, Customs and the DHP StationBeirut, Syria).
60125102-5ebb-5175-b8f6-33c1bd1dcafc.description: Beirut Port was part of an integrated maritime and railway complex and the printed title of this postcard specifically identifies the customs facilities and the D.H.P. station. The train tracks run directly along the quay beside warehouses, illustrating the physical connection between maritime shipping and inland railway transport. The railway connection to the Beirut quay, completed in 1903, was intended to facilitate the direct movement of merchandise and reduce intermediate transhipment. The port infrastructure can be placed within the much larger transformation of Eastern Mediterranean commerce, with the nineteenth-century increase in Ottoman-European trade.

601e5d3a-e68f-587a-846c-d0f3657cf4f6.name: *Dar al-Baladiyya, Damascus*
601e5d3a-e68f-587a-846c-d0f3657cf4f6.short_description: Built between 1892 to 1894, the Dar al-Baladiyya was a prestigious edifice in stone. With its neo-classical elements and prominent middle projection, it was designed to display the power of the “new” state. The purpose of building the City Hall was functional, since the administrative workload, which rapidly increased after the reforms of the administrative system had to be accommodated.

61ff0f1e-695e-5970-a8a9-44151ef0e284.name: Traditional peasant attire
61ff0f1e-695e-5970-a8a9-44151ef0e284.short_description: Peasants and ordinary people's clothes did not change much over the centuries. It generally consisted of a shorter, narrower and darker coloured pair of baggy *shirwal* trousers for winter, and another pair in a lighter beige or khaki colour for the summer. This was paired with a cotton shirt or vest, called a *sudriye*, and a short embroidered *abaya*. A *keffiye*, a large scarf made of white cotton, was worn on the head with a *lebbede* or *'agal* on top.
61ff0f1e-695e-5970-a8a9-44151ef0e284.author: Jeff El-Msanne, Hassan El Masri, Remy Nader
keywords: Shirwal; Clothes; Traditions; Keffiye; Colour
materials: The costumes were made of cotton and silk

623ac570-c51d-5c93-af68-2dca3ce23ce0.name: Suspended Together
623ac570-c51d-5c93-af68-2dca3ce23ce0.description: Manal Al Dowayan’s Suspended Together can be used to question the assumption that the existence of roads, routes, and transport systems automatically means freedom of movement. Created in 2011, the installation refers to a period when Saudi women needed permission from a male guardian in order to travel. The suspended white doves suggest flight, mobility, and freedom, yet their stillness reveals a condition of restriction. In this sense, the work is especially relevant for discussing travel and infrastructure from a gendered perspective: even when roads exist, not everyone has equal access to movement. The piece reminds viewers that mobility is not only a matter of physical routes, but also of law, social permission, gender, and power. For this reason, the work can be used to expand a discussion of travel in the region beyond railways and roads, toward the unequal social conditions that determine who is allowed to move.

63e03fb2-ff4b-5263-b342-f74d2b6bdf14.name: La Grande Gare du Hidjaz, Damas (The Grand Railway Station of Hijaz, Damascus)
63e03fb2-ff4b-5263-b342-f74d2b6bdf14.description: The Hijaz Railway Station building is one of several major public buildings established during the late Ottoman period under the rule of Sultan Abdülhamid II in Damascus. The construction was carried out under the supervision of Hüseyin Nazım Pasha, the Wali (Governor) of Damascus and chairman of the committee responsible for implementing the Hijaz Railway project. He oversaw the plan to construct the railway between Damascus and Medina from 1900 to 1908, mobilising conscripts and civilian labour to participate in its construction, while also benefiting from the expertise of German engineers and other foreign specialists who came to supervise the railway project.

640180dd-059b-54fe-a33c-0700c3dd70f8.name: Photograph of the Beirut–Aleppo railway
640180dd-059b-54fe-a33c-0700c3dd70f8.short_description: The second railway built in Lebanon opened in 1906 and ran from Beirut to Aleppo in present-day Syria. It connected with the first railway line at Riyaq. The connection between Aleppo and Beirut, a well-equipped and sizeable port, decreased trade in Alexandretta, the traditional port for merchandise leaving or entering Syria. Alexandretta was not connected to Aleppo by rail until 1914. Aleppo and Northern Syria became increasingly important as links between Damascus and Beirut were consolidated. This also marked the increasing importance of Beirut as a powerful city in the region and not only as a Mediterranean port.
640180dd-059b-54fe-a33c-0700c3dd70f8.author: Hady El Hajj, Jennifer Harb, Cynthia Karaki
keywords: Transport; Railway; Communication; Connection; Innovation; Aleppo; Lebanon

6407ba69-5120-5550-9850-d55a3019a722.name: Railway construction works
6407ba69-5120-5550-9850-d55a3019a722.description: The Giaurdere Viaduct, its name during construction, is now known as the Varda Viaduct and was constructed near Hacıkırı in the Taurus Mountains. Built between 1907 and 1912 for the Baghdad Railway, the bridge follows a curved alignment across a deep ravine and rises about 99 metres above the valley floor over a length of roughly 172 metres. It was built by Philipp Holzmann A.G. Architecturally, the viaduct (long, high bridge with a series of arches) combines monumental stone-clad piers with three principal arches and shorter approach spans. The tall, lattice supports reduce the structure’s visual mass while carrying the railway deck high above the irregular terrain; the repeated arches create a strong, stable structure across the valley. The photograph also shows the temporary lower bridge, which was used as an alternative line until the finish of the construction and to transport stone, steel, workers and machinery before the permanent crossing could operate.

670372b2-f67e-5ac4-8b1b-28c10cd4bd8e.name: Section of a rail from Hijaz Railway with commemorative inscription
670372b2-f67e-5ac4-8b1b-28c10cd4bd8e.description: In September 1900, Sultan Abdul Hamid addressed a call for all Muslims all over the world to collect donations to establish a railway between Damascus and the holy places to facilitate transporting the pilgrims. The call was responded to enthusiastically and with the great support of all Muslims. The cost of the project was estimated at approximately five million Ottoman golden lira which were provided from: donations, the revenues of the Ottoman State earned from the sale of the stamps, and a special tax upon all the citizens for the railway. Construction of the narrow-gauge track (105cm) whose axle weight was (10.5 tonnes) began in 1900 with a wire telegraph line along its side connecting Damascus with Medina across Amman with a total track length of 1303km. The construction of the project ended in 1908. All the tracks and the stations were completed as detailed below: Mezerib Dera'a section, September 1901; Dera'a Al-Zarqa section, September 1902; Al-Zarqa Amman section, September 1903; Amman Ma'an section, September 1904; Ma'an Tabuk section, end of 1906; Tabuk Medain Saleh, September 1907; Medain Saleh Medina, September 1908. These rails were brought from the destroyed railroad tracks that were harmed by Arab revolt army attacks in 1917. On one side of the first rail is an Arabic phrase written in divan script: "*min khayrat mawlana Amir al-mu'minin al-sultan al-ghazi 'abdal-hamid khan thani 'azza nasruhu*".

679af2a1-a210-5f1f-927c-cd4ef3b1d0b4.name: Iron bridge near Haifa
679af2a1-a210-5f1f-927c-cd4ef3b1d0b4.description: This album of 39 images documents the construction of the Hijaz Railway. It photographs two important stretches of the network: the route between Damascus and Maʿan, and the line connecting Daraʿa with Haifa. Its photographs record the remarkable engineering achievements required to negotiate difficult and varied terrain, while also illustrating the railway’s role in strengthening connections across the empire. Alongside tunnels, bridges and stations, the images capture the engineers, officials and labourers whose work made the project possible.

6c402e37-2b9b-5950-a717-adb9b30770b5.name: Church of the Tomb of Mary.
6c402e37-2b9b-5950-a717-adb9b30770b5.description:
The Virgin Mary, the mother of Christ, has an important and significant place in Islamic doctrine. There is an entire chapter in the Holy Qur'an that bears the name of Mary, in addition to her being considered the highest exemplar of the virtues of chastity and purity in the Islamic culture.  
The historian, Al-Hanbali (d. AH 928 / AD 1522) mentions that the grave of the Virgin Mary was in a church famous as a place of pilgrimage for both Christians and Muslims. He mentioned that when the Caliph ‘Umar Ibn al-Khattab (r. AH 13-23 / AD 634–44) visited Jerusalem after the conquest of AH 17 / AD 638, he passed by the Church of Mary and prayed two *rak'ats* in it. The pan-faith significance of the church serves as an explanation as to why there is a large *mihrab* to the south of the tomb.  
The origin of the building was a natural cave, upon which a Byzantine church was erected in AD 582 - 602. The church was built on two levels and bore the name of Mary, Mother of Christ. In the course of time the church deteriorated and another was built to replace it. The traveller, Arculf described the Western-style roof of the church in around AH 49–50 / AD 670. The Crusaders undertook the rebuilding of the present church on their arrival in Jerusalem. Despite the fact that the four Gospels do not mention either the death or the place of burial of the Virgin Mary, Eastern Christian tradition considers the location of the church to be where the Virgin Mary is buried and where she made her ascent to heaven.  
The entrance to the church is preceded by an open courtyard with a square plan. There is a 5 m drop from the public pathway into the church portal, negotiated by way of a descending staircase. The entrance has a great rectangular door above which there is a pointed stone arch built in the Gothic-Crusader style. The entrance leads to a long and broad vaulted staircase area, which descends in 47 marble stairs. The vaulted area is roofed with a series of consecutive arches supported by intersecting vaults that dominate the building. At the end of the vaulted area lies the tomb of the Virgin Mary; originating as a cave, part of the architectural fabric is excavated from rock, while some has been built. The shrine descends 12 m from the level of the church entrance. The tomb is a carved block of rock that lies at the centre of the eastern section of the cave. In this form, it resembles the tomb of Jesus in the middle of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. To the south of the grave there is a large undecorated *mihrab* crowned by a dome.
6c402e37-2b9b-5950-a717-adb9b30770b5.short_description: The church is located to the east of the old city. Its construction was undertaken in the late Byzantine period at a cavern that was considered to be the grave of the Virgin Mary, who occupies a distinguished place in both Islam and Christianity. The present building goes back to the Crusader period and is in the Gothic style. Little remains of the architectural elements of the former churches at this site. The site is also sacred to Muslims and the church contains a number of *mihrab*s (niches).
6c402e37-2b9b-5950-a717-adb9b30770b5.dates: Beginning of Hegira 6th century / AD 12th century.
6c402e37-2b9b-5950-a717-adb9b30770b5.method_for_datation: The church is dated by information concerning the site, which is further supported by primary historical sources.

6c4a7fd1-e659-525c-ad3d-c6180e7f9ebe.name: Palästina. Haifa. Panorama (Palestine)
6c4a7fd1-e659-525c-ad3d-c6180e7f9ebe.description: A panoramic view of Haifa’s coastline is shown in this postcard. The city developed into an important Mediterranean outlet of the Hijaz Railway after the construction of the Daraa–Haifa branch in the early twentieth century. Once the line connected the Syrian interior and the Hauran with the coast, Haifa gained a more important role in regional trade and transportation. Haifa Station and railway construction were part of a broader Ottoman programme of urban and infrastructural development in the city.

6c5debca-9932-5c4a-89ab-f8f3d13de354.name: Dinar
6c5debca-9932-5c4a-89ab-f8f3d13de354.description: Gold Dinar of Hijaz, King Hussein bin 'Ali, AH 1334. On November, 1916 the notables, ulama of Hijaz and a majority of the sheiks of Bedouins and sedentary tribes, assembled at the great Mosque of Mecca to pay allegiance to al-Hussein and proclaim him “King“ of Arab Countries. On this occasion a coin bearing his name at Mecca, as King of the Arabs was struck. But Britain, France and Italy recognized him only as “King of the Hijaz” on 3 January 1917. On obverse: "*bi-l-bilad al-'arabiyya al-husayn bin 'ali / 'abduhu / hashimi / wa ibn 'abdihi / al-nahidh*" ("Hussein bin Ali / God’s Servant / Hashimi /and son of God’s Servant / leader of Arab renaissance"). On reverse: "*duriba bi-makka al-mukarrama / sana 1334 / dinar / sana 8 / 'asima al-hukuma al-'arabiyya*" ("Dinar minted at Makka al-Mukarrama in 1334 \[AH\] in the reign year 8 capital of Arab Government"). All regular coins of Hijaz bear the accessional date of ١٣٣٤ (AH 1334) of al-Hussein bin 'Ali, plus the regional year, many bronze coins had a light silver wash.
6c5debca-9932-5c4a-89ab-f8f3d13de354.author: Aida Naghawi

6cd47255-25d3-54ce-a323-50d1b8890c29.name: La Gare du Hijaz, Damas (The Hijaz Railway Station, Damascus)
6cd47255-25d3-54ce-a323-50d1b8890c29.description: The Hijaz Station in Damascus, originally known locally as Qanawat Station, was originally built in 1903 and later became the main starting point of the Hijaz  Railway linking Damascus with Medina. In 1912, a competition was organised to select a new design for the Hijaz Station. As a result, the new building designed by the Spanish architect Fernando de Aranda was opened to the public in 1917. The design was a combination of historicism and Rococo, with local architectural elements like Ablaq and ornamentation like Ajami.

6e13aca8-8a19-574f-8378-12aea190e022.name: File 3142/1903 'Hedjaz Railway'
6e13aca8-8a19-574f-8378-12aea190e022.description:
This volume contains copies of correspondence between British officials regarding the construction of the Hijaz Railway. The correspondence discusses a number of different aspects of the railway including its route, the progress of its construction and donations made towards its construction by members of the Muslim community in India.  
  
A limited amount of the correspondence in the volume is in French, including a copy of a letter sent by Paul Cambon, the French Ambassador in London, to Sir Edward Grey, the Foreign Secretary (folio 15).  
  
The volume contains a number of reports and related information about the railway. Of particular interest are the following:  
  
A report on the Hijaz Railway by Major Francis Richard Maunsell, dated July 1907 (ff 56-69)  
A memorandum respecting German influence on the Hijaz Railway by George Ambrose Lloyd, 1906 (ff 95-96)  
A list of the principal stations on the Hijaz Railway with approximate distances between Damascus and each station (f 100)  
A map of the Hijaz Railway with list of stations (f 106)  
A report by Mr Teofani Loiso, Vice-Consul at Mersina, based on information provided to him by his son who was employed as an engineer on the railway (ff 105-107)  
A report by Herr Otto von Kapp Kohlstein, a German engineer who inspected the Haifa-Damascus branch of the route and worked on the construction of the Damascus-Maan branch (ff 107-109).  
In addition, the volume contains cuttings (and translations) of press articles related to several aspects of the railway and its construction. Also included are two maps. The Turkish (Ottoman) language material consists of the second of these two maps.  
  
The volume includes a divider which gives the year that the subject file was opened, the subject heading, and a list of correspondence references contained in it arranged by year. This divider is placed at the front of the volume.

6e6660f9-03e5-571b-ac42-c15308782f3e.name: The Great ‘Umari Mosque
6e6660f9-03e5-571b-ac42-c15308782f3e.description:
The Great ‘Umari Mosque measuring 66.5 m. × 65.5 m., is a composite of several architectural styles that developed during various successive periods; the most important of which was the Mamluk period. The mosque was largely ruined during the Second World War, although the Supreme Islamic Council renovated it in 1924.  
  
The oldest part of the mosque, which has a basilica plan, dates to the Crusader period. This was the Cathedral dedicated to St John the Baptist, which was built on the site of the Friday Mosque, and was in the city centre during the early Islamic period. It consists of a central nave flanked by two aisles, all covered with cross vaults. The main entrance portal is on its west wall, above which is a circular window. The design of the portal with its columns, capitals and arches are in the Gothic style. On either side of the nave is a row of pillars and composite Byzantine marble columns crowned with what seem to be re-used Corinthian capitals.  
  
After the Crusaders departed the city in 583/1187, the building was converted into a Friday Mosque, and thus regained its old name: the “‘Umari Mosque”. In the Mamluk period, Sultan al-Mansur Husam al-Din Lajin (696/1297–698/1299) added to the mosque the eastern portal, which leads directly into the central nave of the early building (the basilica), and a minaret. The latter collapsed as a result of an earthquake, but was rebuilt before the First World War. The amir Sunqur al-‘Ala’i, the Viceroy of Gaza in 697/1297–1298, supervised the renovation works. He added a window and a portal to the northern wall of the basilica.  
  
The Amir Tankiz al-Nasiri, the Viceroy of Syria, supervised the second main additions to the building in 730/1329–1330. The basilica’s southern wall was removed and an additional aisle, in the style of the Crusader period, was added. Another entrance portal to the mosque was built in the southern wall, which leads to al-Qaysariyya (the Gold Market) and which also once led to Khan al-Zayt, which no longer exists.  
  
To the north of the old building is a courtyard surrounded by porticoes from the east, west and south. The southern portico, which was built in the 11th/17th century, faces the courtyard through a triple-arched colonnade, and is covered by three cross vaults with shallow domes. The eastern and western corridors were built at the end of the 12th/18th century. In the southern portico, there is a Mamluk-period minbar and a mihrab, both of which were moved from the Mosque of Sultan Qaytbay. The western entrance portal, and a number of the porticoes that lie behind it, were constructed at the end of the 13th/19th century.
keywords: Gaza; Great ‘Umari Mosque; Mosque; Friday Mosque; St John the Baptist Cathedral;  Palestine

70532759-69a2-50fb-9785-96449e6c4250.name: Information book for the Syrian Hejaz railway
70532759-69a2-50fb-9785-96449e6c4250.description: This rare document provides crucial insight into the Hijaz Railway during the Arab Revolt led by T.E. Lawrence. It outlines essential regulations regarding train operations and communication, highlighting the railway's strategic role in disrupting Ottoman reinforcements. This manual also explores the logistical challenges of wartime, contributing to our understanding of military strategy and railway operations.

713a80ee-86ad-5103-bcf7-5c70eb44eb3b.name: The interior of Tabuk Hospital
713a80ee-86ad-5103-bcf7-5c70eb44eb3b.short_description: In 1900 the Ottoman Sultan Abdülhamid II (r.1876–1909) began the construction of a railway line connecting Damascus to the holy cities of Medina and Mecca. Built by public subscription and with an appeal to Muslims of the world for financial support, the railway line reached Medina in 1908, but didn't reach Mecca. It was built with the assistance of German engineers who worked closely with Turkish officials. This album of the Hijaz Railway probably belonged to a Turkish engineer who worked on the construction of the line. It has 50 photographs, mostly of stations and sections of the line, but also of the landscape that the line passed through in the area between Tabuk and Mada’in Salih. The photographs were most likely taken by J. H. Halladjian, an Armenian photographer with a studio in Haifa in Palestine active in the 1890s and early 20th century. Based on records at the Imperial War Museum and The Royal Geographical Society, Halladjian took photographs of the Hijaz Railway and places along its route. The album contains some important photographs such as the one of the hospital at Tabuk which was established in 1907 and which became the railway’s quarantine station (ARC.al 6.16) as well as images which demonstrate the hardship of cutting through rock in order to pass the line through mountainous terrain (ARC.al 6.24). Also documented here are the great stone monoliths north of Mada'in Salih (ARC.al 6.38) in Mabrak al Naga, where prior to the Hijaz Railway, the Ottoman government connected the Hijaz to Istanbul via a telegraph line which reached Mada'in Salih in 1900. The building of the overland telegraph line between Damascus and Medina, much like the construction of the Hijaz Railway project to follow, was fraught with complications including the terrain and the danger of Bedouin resistance.

71d76fc5-c9ad-524d-9391-c2dd24da5ac5.name: Chemin de fer, Postcard, Alep (Aleppo Railway Station)
71d76fc5-c9ad-524d-9391-c2dd24da5ac5.description: This composite postcard presents Aleppo’s earlier railway complex, generally identified as Damascus Station, together with a separate building labelled Pavillon militaire. Located in the Jamiliyeh district of Aleppo, the station served the French-operated railway Damas, Hama et Prolongements (D.H.P.), linking Aleppo southward through Hama and Homs with Damascus. The Hama–Aleppo extension entered service in 1906. The upper image shows a restrained two-storey masonry station with a long covered platform, regularly spaced windows and numerous chimneys, reflecting its combined passenger, administrative and possibly staff functions. The lower image records the military pavilion, with a raised entrance, deep tiled roofs and an ornamental timber porch distinguish it from the station building.

7281683b-fda9-593c-917d-2afe6e08c7b6.name: Building a bridge near Haifa
7281683b-fda9-593c-917d-2afe6e08c7b6.description: This album of 39 images documents the construction of the Hijaz Railway. It photographs two important stretches of the network: the route between Damascus and Maʿan, and the line connecting Daraʿa with Haifa. Its photographs record the remarkable engineering achievements required to negotiate difficult and varied terrain, while also illustrating the railway’s role in strengthening connections across the empire. Alongside tunnels, bridges and stations, the images capture the engineers, officials and labourers whose work made the project possible.

72a638fd-b169-554c-b04b-445c6aa0fa3e.name: Bab al-Khalil (Gate of Hebron).
72a638fd-b169-554c-b04b-445c6aa0fa3e.description:
The Bab al-Khalil (Gate of Hebron) is the only gate that receives visitors into the city of Jerusalem from both the south and the west. It is for this reason that the gate was given two names: Bab Hebron (al-Khalil) and Bab Yaffa (Jaffa), as they are two cities located to the south and west of the gate. Roughly facing Bab al-Khalil is Bab al-Asbat (the Lion's Gate), located in the east wall of the old city of Jerusalem.  
Due to the architectural bulk of Bab al-Khalil it resembles a tower projecting from the fortified walls. The gate is square in design and contains an L-shaped passageway whereby the orientation of both the interior and exterior are forced to change direction by an angle of 90 degrees. This layout is reminiscent of other gates in the walls of Jerusalem and similar gates of the Middle Ages, specifically those of the Mamluk and Ottoman periods.  
The interior of the gate is accessed by an entrance on the north side of the wall. The entrance leads into a vestibule, on the west wall of which is an aperture with an embrasure opening. An inscription panel hangs in the middle of the south side of the vestibule, recording the name of the Ottoman Sultan, Sulayman the Magnificent as patron of the fortifications.  
The northern side of Bab al-Khalil leads into the city by means of a wide receding portal that ends with a supporting arch. Directly above the arch is an inscription panel carved in Ottoman *naskhi* script:  
“In the Name of the God, the Most Gracious and the Most Merciful,  
The order for the construction of these blessed walls was made by our master, the Sultan the Great, The Sovereign, The Ruler of Rome, Arabs and Persians, Sultan Sulayman bin Selim Khan. May God prolong his reign and power in the year AH 945 \[AD 1538\].”  
The portal is flanked by a recess, above which is a tapered arch. Around the voussoirs of the arch there is stamped decoration. The decoration ends either side of the arch with a projecting panel in the form of a medallion carved with vegetal and geometric motifs. At the height of one stone course from the keystone of the arch there is a stone lobe. Directly above it are three stone corbels, which bear a machicolation. Opening out of this façade, is an embrasure for shooting arrows as well as serving as an observation point. The eastern façade of Bab al-Khalil, which overlooks the interior of the city, resembles the northern façade of the gate.
72a638fd-b169-554c-b04b-445c6aa0fa3e.short_description: This is the only gate which opens onto the Western Wall of Jerusalem. Its construction was ordered by Sultan Sulayman the Magnificent as part of his great project to restore the walls of the city and its gates. For defence purposes the two vestibules of the gate are at right angles to each other, meeting at a sharp corner. An inscription panel is set in the middle of the southern façade which records the name of the sultan as the builder of the gate and the walls of Jerusalem. The gate also has other elements whose aim is to facilitate its defence.
72a638fd-b169-554c-b04b-445c6aa0fa3e.method_for_datation: The gate is dated by epigraphic inscriptions on both its interior walls and northern façade.

742e675b-2783-5254-a6e4-abd2e2dc3cd3.name: *Monument commemorating the installation of the Hijaz-Damascus telegraph connection, Damascus*
742e675b-2783-5254-a6e4-abd2e2dc3cd3.short_description: This monument is a well-known benchmark, which remained the symbol of the municipal administration until a few years ago. The bronze column in the middle of the Merje Square was erected in commemoration of the Istanbul-Damascus-Mecca telegraph link. It was the line with the sultan’s Islamist policy, acting as a symbol of the Ottoman claim to leadership over Muslims. The monumental telegraph column is crowned by a model of the Istanbul Hamidiye Mosque, where every week the Sultan ‘Abdülhamid [`Abd al-Hamid II] had his visit to the mosque for Friday prayers celebrated with an imperial march-past- a demonstration of the concentrated political power of the Sultan.

74e859d1-c1c6-5807-b47d-520e455a5953.name: Madrasa al-Ashrafiyya
74e859d1-c1c6-5807-b47d-520e455a5953.description:
The Madrasa al-Ashrafiyya is renowned as the most splendid in Jerusalem, not only for its architecture and artistic design, but also as being the most important educational institution. The historian Mujir al-Din al-Hanbali 901/1496 described it as the third jewel in Jerusalem’s crown after the Aqsa Mosque and the Dome of the Rock. It is named after the Mamluk Sultan al-Ashraf Qaytbay, who rebuilt it between 885/1480–887/1482 – hence it is also called the al-Sultaniyya Madrasa.  
  
Demolished and rebuilt, the madrasa was initially constructed during the reign of Sultan al-Dahir Khushqadam by the Amir Hassan al-Dahiri, who was the Inspector of the two Haram sites between 869/1464 and 872/1467. He died before it was completed, so the Amir Hassan al-Dahiri transferred the building to Sultan Qaytbay. The latter commissioned the Amir Bardabak al-Taji, who had become the new Inspector of the two Harams, to complete the construction. It was finally finished in 875/1470, as indicated on the inscription plaque that is still on the old wall of the madrasa near Bab al-Silsila. The official inauguration date was 877/1472, when the sultan appointed Shihab al-Din al-‘Umari, as the shaykh of the madrasa and employed a number of sufi scholars to teach there. He also bestowed a generous waqf upon it. Mujir al-Din al-‘Umari mentions that he allocated enough funding to cover the salaries of 60 sufis (45 dirhams each per month), a shaykh, (500 dirhams per month) and many other employees, plus the running costs of the institution. Included in his waqf were 28 villages in Gaza, Ramla, Jerusalem and Hebron, and a caravanserai, a hammam, two presses, a mill, a bakery, a stable, and shops and houses in Gaza.  
  
When Sultan Qaytbay saw the madrasa for the first time in 880/1475, he was deeply disappointed as it looked the same as other buildings in the Haram, and he ordered it to be destroyed. He commissioned a group of Egyptian architects and craftsmen to build it under the auspices of a Coptic architect. When it was completed in 887/1482, it was considered to be a masterpiece of Mamluk architecture and no other madrasa in Jerusalem could rival it. This was confirmed in the description of the well-known Dominican priest Felix Fabry who visited it in 888/1484. Sadly, a large part of the madrasa was demolished in 903/1497–1498 when an earthquake hit the city, although it was rebuilt and renovated according to its original plan.The madrasa’s educational activities continued for three centuries and many travellers and historians who had visited it between the 10th/16th and 11th/17th centuries, marvelled at its beauty. The Turkish traveller, Evlia Çelebi described it in 1080/1669–1670: “The Madrasa al-Sultaniyya is the best madrasa in Jerusalem”. The sufi scholar ‘Abd al-Ghani al-Nabulsi stayed there in 1102/1690–1691 and described it as a great madrasa of immense importance.  
  
The Madrasa al-Ashrafiyya consists of two storeys. The main entrance portal of the building, accessed from the Haram’s courtyard, is distinguished by lavish architectural and ornamental details and is the epitome of Mamluk art and architecture. It has a porch open on both its southern and eastern sides, which is supported by two pointed arches that are covered by a fan-shaped vault. The door is set in a deep recess covered by a semi-dome that is carved and lavishly decorated with glazed ceramic tiles. The door leads into a vestibule that ends in a large assembly hall to the north. Two windows and a door on the eastern wall of this hall overlook the Haram’s courtyard. Its northern wall also has a window and a door, while the southern wall has a window and a colourful decorated mihrab.  
  
Today, the hall serves as a workshop for the conservation of the Haram’s manuscripts and documents. To the south of the vestibule lies a stone staircase that leads to the upper floor and to the minaret above Bab al-Silsila. The southern part of this floor is ruined, although its Mamluk layout can still be observed, representative of the Mamluk four-iwans cruciform plan. In the centre there is a courtyard surrounded by two main iwans in the north and south, and two smaller iwans in the east and west. Of these four iwans, only the southern one has survived, with its mihrab. The south-west part of this storey has a number of rooms that today form part of a school for the religious education of girls.
keywords: Jerusalem; Madrasa al-Ashrafiyya; Sultan al-Ashraf Qaytbay; Mamluk architecture

74efc106-e576-5569-bfb1-3b51d81c8622.name: Church of the Holy Sepulchre.
74efc106-e576-5569-bfb1-3b51d81c8622.description:
The Church of the Holy Sepulchre enjoys a rich history and has extraordinarily distinguished artistic and architectural traits. The church is sacred to all the Christian faiths as, as is evident from the name, it is revered as the site of the Resurrection of Jesus following his Crucifixion, his suffering and death. According to Christian belief Jesus was buried (the sepulchre) in this church. The Church of the Holy Sepulchre is a large architectural complex that includes a number of smaller chapels; in total the area exceeds 5000 sq m.  
When the first church was founded on this site during the Byzantine period it included four elements: atrium, basilica, open courtyard and the sepulchre or holy tomb. In AD 614 the Persians set fire to the church, badly damaging it; the church was repeatedly thereinafter partially destroyed and repaired over the next 400 years. The Patriarch, Modestus undertook restoration of the church following the attack, and made alterations to it, decreasing the scale of the original plan. The Caliph 'Umar Ibn al-Khattab (r. AH 13–23 / AD 634–4), who was notoriously protective of Christian sites, refused to pray in the church when the Patriarch Sophronius suggested he did so; apparently he was eager to protect the city's Christian rights.  
The Crusaders made alterations and additions to the church, the initial implementation of which had been the ambitious project of Constantine IX Monomachos and which transformed the design of the church once again. A new church was erected in AH 543 / AD 1149, which was known as the Church of Nisf al-Dunya (Church at the Centre of the Universe, a catholicon used by monks), in the Romanesque style. The church was built around the rocky hill of the Crucifixion, the Rock of Calvary (Golgotha) overlooking the Rotunda. Similarly, the alterations included those made to the entrance leading to the place of Crucifixion within the church building, while the level underneath it was made the burial place of some of the Frankish kings. A bell tower, the doors of which opened to the south instead of the east, was added in AH 566 / AD 1170. Despite these important changes, the most prominent features of the Church remained until AH 583 / AD 1187. Saladin followed the example of 'Umar Ibn al-Khattab and was tolerant of Christians and respected their rights to worship.  
Entrance to the church is by way of a great portal, above which there is a huge stone lintel. The lintel is carved with decoration in low relief portraying scenes from the Bible. On entering the portal, there is a modern staircase that leads up to the site of the Crucifixion, which today is divided into two sections: east and west. What remains of the Rock of Calvary is found in the west-facing Greek area surrounded by a glass frame. The Rock is cracked and according to the Christian faith the crack occurred when Christ was stabbed by a Roman soldier and was stripped of his cloak.  
A descending staircase confronts the ascending stairwell and leads to the Stone of Anointing where, to the west of the Stone, a wall has been erected that divides the entrance from the Church of Nisf al-Dunya. A little to the south is the holy dome covered by a large semi-circular stone dome with a cylindrical drum supported by a series of pillars. A central window opens onto the pivot of the dome, which is decorated with 12 petals in gold leaf, symbolising the 12 apostles of Christ. In addition to those areas discussed here, there are a number of other cells, rooms, halls and chapels in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre.
74efc106-e576-5569-bfb1-3b51d81c8622.short_description: This holiest of holy Christian sites is revered as the site of the tomb and Resurrection of Jesus Christ. It is set almost in the centre of the old city of Jerusalem. The church is a great complex that includes a number of chapels, oratories, cloisters and subterranean chambers and holds many icons, mosaics and important religious statues. Renovations since its original construction has given it stylistic variety and it is now predominantly in the Romanesque and Gothic. The church has number of divisions which are imperceptible except by the religious raiment of each Christian sect that controls that section.
74efc106-e576-5569-bfb1-3b51d81c8622.dates: The first construction AD 326-335. The present construction inaugurated in AH 543 / AD 1149.
74efc106-e576-5569-bfb1-3b51d81c8622.method_for_datation: The building was dated by means of historical sources.
74efc106-e576-5569-bfb1-3b51d81c8622.bibliography: Al-Natsheh, Y., *Kanisat al-Qiyama \[Church of the Holy Sepulchre*\], Jerusalem, 2002.
74efc106-e576-5569-bfb1-3b51d81c8622.patrons: Emperor Constantine (r. AD 308–37) and his mother, Helena.
74efc106-e576-5569-bfb1-3b51d81c8622.architects: The construction was supervised by Qasis of Constantinople, also known as Eustathius. The engineer/designer was known as Zanobious from Palmyra (today Tadmur in Syria).
74efc106-e576-5569-bfb1-3b51d81c8622.dynasty: The church dates back to the Byzantine period but several renovations were implemented in subsequent periods.
74efc106-e576-5569-bfb1-3b51d81c8622.author: Yusuf al-Natsheh
keywords: Resurrection; Crucifixion; church; Jesus

752b7f53-4c79-5513-bbe6-c8c51b39c873.name: German Jildirim photocard
752b7f53-4c79-5513-bbe6-c8c51b39c873.description: The photographic postcard shows merchants with loaded camels alongside a railway freight yard. The scene documents an important commercial dimension of the Hijaz Railway. Alongside pilgrims and soldiers, the line transported merchandise between regional markets and contributed to increased economic and trading activity. Rail transport did not immediately replace camel caravans. Camels continued to bring agricultural produce and other loads from villages, pastoral areas and routes beyond the tracks to railway stations, where goods could be transferred to wagons for longer-distance shipment. Historians therefore describe animal transport as a feeder to the late Ottoman railway network rather than simply its outdated rival. During the First World War, this combined system became still more important, since trains carried bulk freight along fixed routes while camels supplied places beyond the railway. The seated men and water pipe also reveal the freight yard as a social space of waiting, work and exchange, bringing together traders, animal handlers and railway infrastructure.

75686fa8-f38a-5ba8-bc38-088996a3046a.name: Photographic postcard of Jannat al-Baqi‘, Medina
75686fa8-f38a-5ba8-bc38-088996a3046a.short_description: These photographic postcards when joined together form a panoramic view of al-Baqi‘ graveyard in Medina. Otherwise known as ‘*Baqi‘al-Gharqad*’ this graveyard is on the south-eastern side of the Prophet's Mosque and was a site chosen by the Prophet Muhammad as an exclusive Muslim cemetery. It is known as the oldest and most important historical Islamic graveyard. Many of the Prophet’s companions, family-members and followers are buried there. Although early travel accounts (for example, that of Ibn Jubayr (d. AD 1217)) state that the exact location of many graves had been lost, certainly until 1925, it was possible to locate many important early Muslim graves. For Shiˋa Muslims this is where four of the Shiˋi imams are buried, making it a special place of visitation. In this panoramic, the buildings which had been constructed over significant graves are identifiable. The larger building visible in ARC.pc 401 is the mausoleum the *Ahl al-bayt* (members of the Prophet’s family), while the smaller buildings were known to be the resting-places specifically of the wives and children of the Prophet. The buildings and tombstones no longer exist as they were destroyed by the Wahhabis under Ibn Saud in 1926. The original photographs were taken by a Turkish photographer for Bernhard Moritz, a Professor of Oriental Languages in Berlin, during his travels in the Middle East between 1905 and 1915. They were first published in *Bilder aus Palästina, Nord-Arabien und dem Sinai* (Images from Palestine, North Arabia, and the Sinai) which contains 105 photographs of the Middle East and published by Moritz in 1916.

76a3eee4-0751-522b-aba2-407457b8b9e2.name: Hamidi Hospital (Mashfa al-Ghuraba)
76a3eee4-0751-522b-aba2-407457b8b9e2.description: The Hamidi Hospital (Mashfa al-Ghuraba, or Hospital of Strangers) was established in Damascus during the reign of Ottoman Sultan Abdülhamid II. The hospital opened in 1317 AH (1900), west of the Suleymaniye Takiyya. It was built by the Damascus municipality, financed through public donations, municipal revenues, and endowments previously supporting the Nuri Hospital. Its establishment formed part of the expansion of modern medical institutions in late Ottoman Damascus. The hospital was associated with medical provision for Ottoman soldiers and workers on the Hijaz Railway. In 1903, an imperial decree authorised the establishment of a medical school on the hospital's grounds, and the school was later moved into its own building in 1914.  The Hospital was renamed the National Hospital during the period of the short-lived Arab government following Ottoman rule. The building was subsequently restored and adapted into the Rida Said Conference Centre of Damascus University, opened in September 2003.

776b254f-37bf-5617-8d2b-3b37c80ca73f.name: San Remo: The Conference of the Four Nations
776b254f-37bf-5617-8d2b-3b37c80ca73f.description: San Remo Conference, April 1920. Held after World War I, this conference brought together Britain, France, Italy and Japan to decide the fate of former Ottoman lands. Britain received mandates over Palestine and Mesopotamia (later Iraq), while France gained Syria and Lebanon. Rooted in the Sykes–Picot plan and the Balfour Declaration, these decisions also determined the future of Ottoman infrastructure such as the Hijaz Railway. Strikingly, no representatives from the region were present and the map of the Middle East was redrawn without local voices.
776b254f-37bf-5617-8d2b-3b37c80ca73f.artist: Meurisse Press Agency. Photographic agency (commissioning body).

79bec849-104d-5cdc-a478-1cfc829ea187.name: Les Ponts du Chemin de fer près de Doummar, Syrie (Doummar Railway Bridges, Syria)
79bec849-104d-5cdc-a478-1cfc829ea187.description: Dummar was one of the final stations on the Beirut–Damascus railway before the line reached Damascus-Baramkeh. It is situated approximately seven kilometres by rail from the terminus, after the stations of the Barada valley and immediately before Damascus. The postcard, captioned "Les Ponts du Chemin de fer près de Doummar", focuses on the railway infrastructure and shows the track curving across a bridge through the densely wooded landscape surrounding the Dummar region. In the early 1930s, a cement factory was established at Dummar, close to the railway and Dummar station. Its location allowed the industrial complex to make use of the railway infrastructure.

7a4c7957-3c46-5a9b-be58-3644319f261c.name: Hijaz Railway ticket
7a4c7957-3c46-5a9b-be58-3644319f261c.description: Passenger services contributed roughly half of the Hijaz Railway’s total income. The majority of travellers used third-class accommodation, while only around five percent could afford first-class tickets. Up until AH 1331/ AD 1913, second-class compartments were not provided. Despite the railway’s reputation for its route to Madinah, the busiest passenger traffic was actually found on the Haifa–Damascus line, which passed through more densely populated regions. This route offered a daily service that took about 12 hours to complete, with passengers heading south transferring at Deraa.

7ab5bd97-3948-5e4a-9db2-309afc5b078e.name: A lithographed postcard showing Sharif Makka al-kabir Aun ar-Rafiq (ʿAwn al-Rafiq, Grand Sharif of Mecca)
7ab5bd97-3948-5e4a-9db2-309afc5b078e.description: The figure is Sharif ʿAwn al-Rafiq Pasha, who served as Sharif and Emir of Mecca from 1882 until his death in 1905. Institutional catalogues of his surviving portrait consistently identify him by this name and term of office. The title, “Sharif of Mecca”, referred to the Hasanid descendants of the Prophet Muhammad who governed Mecca. Sharifian government in the city developed from the tenth century and remained one of the most important institutions of western Hijaz politics for centuries. As a member of the Hashemite ʿAwn household, he governed the holy city, exercised authority connected with the Hajj, and negotiated his position with the Ottoman administration, whose recognition remained essential to the sharifate. The Arabic heading was intended to identify him as "Sharif Makka al-kabir Aun ar-Rafiq"(ʿAwn al-Rafiq, Grand Sharif of Mecca), but the name is irregularly and inaccurately written on the card as "Sharif al-Makka al-kabir Aun ar-Rabay".

7f1db941-399d-5b93-be52-3e4334ec577f.name: La Gare de Cadem, Damas (The Station of Cadem, Damascus)
7f1db941-399d-5b93-be52-3e4334ec577f.description: The Qadam Station in Damascus was part of the Hijaz Railway, located in Qadam district south of the city centre. The name Qadam (foot) derives from a local Islamic tradition associated with the Prophet Muhammad. The site was believed to mark the place where the Prophet dismounted from his camel during one of his journeys, leaving his footprint impressed on a stone. It was the main departure station for Mecca for several years, and until 1908, pilgrims to Mecca and Medina embarked at the station. They then transferred to the Hijaz Railway Station in central Damascus. The Qadam station remained important for transporting goods and was equipped with sidings, goods sheds, loading facilities and workshops serving the operations.

80bf7d8a-befa-587f-8452-207110b874a9.name: Map of the Sykes–Picot Agreement and Historical Note
80bf7d8a-befa-587f-8452-207110b874a9.description: The lines drawn on the map and the lines drawn in the portrait bear the marks of the same authority: both the border and the identity are shaped by the tip of the pen. During the First World War, Britain and France secretly agreed, with Russia’s approval, to divide the Ottoman Middle East. With a few strokes of the pen, new frontiers were drawn across the lands once linked by the Hijaz Railway. These lines silenced local voices, fragmented communities and reshaped territories. Decisions made behind closed doors by imperial powers set the political, social and cultural course of the region for generations to come.

83ca2754-e506-5404-be99-4dd9fa3be1e5.name: Information for Passengers: Beirut, Tripoli, Alexandretta
83ca2754-e506-5404-be99-4dd9fa3be1e5.description: This advertisement for the Nairn Transport Company, founded in the 1920s, promotes its six-wheeled Pullman buses crossing the desert between Damascus and Baghdad. With timetables linking Haifa, Beirut and Iraq, the service carried both mail and passengers. More than transport, it symbolised modern mobility under the Mandate system, replacing older caravan and railway routes while reflecting new borders and colonial influence in the Middle East.

8452667b-dc79-566c-8b23-9d0b6af62bc0.name: An illustrated album of architecture, including views of Mecca and Medina
8452667b-dc79-566c-8b23-9d0b6af62bc0.short_description:
This large-format volume, entiled *Entwurf einer historischen Architectur in Abbildung unterschiedener beruehmten Gebaeude des Alterthums* (Project for a History of Architecture through pictures of various important buildings from antiquity and foreign people), by Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach (1656–1723) was published in 1725, a few years after his death. Fischer was an Austrian architect and in 1705 he was appointed imperial court architect for Joseph I.  
The book is considered one of the first to attempt an architectural history of the world. It includes nine Islamic buildings amongst its listing of thirteen ‘*foreign*’ buildings. The line drawings of the Iranian and Ottoman buildings are known to have been sourced from illustrated travellers’ accounts, but the addition of the View of Medina and the View of Mecca are remarkable for their originality. Underneath each picture is engraved explanatory text in German and French and they may be the first representations of Mecca and Medina in a European work.  
The plan of Mecca contains some of the known buildings in the *haram*, which are identified by a key, but there is still much confusion about what they are, and although the general plan must have been taken from Ottoman images available at the time, there is much which is incorrect perhaps in an attempt to exoticise the drawings. The view of Medina on the other hand is almost entirely inaccurate and may have been compiled from oral accounts.

845b837c-4ea7-514d-9566-c311425098ea.name: La Gare de Hedjaz, Damas (The Hijaz Station, Damascus)
845b837c-4ea7-514d-9566-c311425098ea.description: Standing before the Hijaz Railway Station is a small rectangular sabil (public fountain), one of the surviving elements of the station complex. Originally located in the centre of the spacious Hijaz Square, the sabil was later relocated to its present position on the pavement in front of the station. The fountain is designed with four faces, each fitted with a water spout, providing drinking water to the public. It represents a continuation of the Islamic tradition of providing free water within public spaces. A commemorative inscription was added later to honour Dr Muslim al Baroudi, who was killed during the French bombardment of Damascus in 1945 while carrying out his humanitarian duties, making the fountain a memorial integrated into the historic setting of the station.

84d0e24a-757f-5557-8920-19da45663b48.description: This album of 39 images documents the construction of the Hijaz Railway. It photographs two important stretches of the network: the route between Damascus and Maʿan, and the line connecting Daraʿa with Haifa.
