84f6b107-47b2-5cd1-a520-3a4f89856221.name: Umayyad Mosque
84f6b107-47b2-5cd1-a520-3a4f89856221.description:
The Umayyad Mosque was built on the site of the Roman Temple of Jupiter, converted into the Church of St John the Baptist in AD 379. After the Islamic conquest of Damascus, the holy site was shared between the Christians and the Muslims of the city. By the succession of the Umayyad Caliph al-Walid bin Abd al-Malik, the church was demolished and a vast congregational mosque constructed instead. The outer wall of the mosque is formed by the Roman *temenos*, an oblong enclosure with pilastered walls, measuring 158 m x 100 m. Of the mosque's three minarets, the one on the southeastern corner is known as the Jesus Minaret, and the one in the centre of the northern wall is known as Minaret of the Bride; both are dated to the early AH 5th / AD 11th century. The southwest minaret was rebuilt by Sultan Qaytbay after the fire of AH 884 / AD 1479.  
The 122.5 m-long and 50 m-wide rectangular courtyard of the mosque is surrounded by a colonnaded portico (*riwaq*) on three sides. Along the southern wall is a triple-aisled 136 m-long and 37 m-wide prayer hall, a layout reminiscent of Byzantine churches. It is divided by two rows of arcades supported by re-used antique columns with Corinthian capitals. A lavish domed transept cuts the arcades into two equal halves; its court façade distinguished by a monumental gabled entrance in the centre, again evoking Byzantine palaces. At one time glass and gold-leaf mosaics covered all the facades in the courtyard. Only the “Barada mosaic” is preserved, so named after the Barada River in Damascus, depicting a landscape with rivers, trees and architectural structures.  
The portico walls were covered with a 3.5 m-high, coloured marble decoration. Today only a few marble slabs in the corner of the southeastern portico are preserved. It was once topped by the *karma* frieze; a long, undulating vine stem of acanthus scrolls carrying grapes, echoing that of the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem. The fine mosaic, stone carving and marble decorations are all antique elements, revealing continuity with Greco-Roman artistic traditions as well as Byzantine architectural features. These features were combined with an Islamic consciousness predicating the lack of human representation in religious spaces. Such 'conscious eclecticism' is the hallmark of the new Umayyad architectural language.  
The speed of construction of this monumental Umayyad Mosque, along with its brilliant decorations and its rich materials, stood as a challenge to the finest Christian churches and an awe-inspiring status-symbol for the Muslim believers. Like the Mosque at Córdoba, a similarly early masterpiece of sacral Muslim architecture, it became a prototype for the “hypostyle mosque” consisting of a simple, spacious courtyard (*sahn*) articulated by a colonnaded portico (*riwaq*) on three sides, and a covered area for praying (*haram*). The division into three aisles and the transept also became influential for mosque architecture throughout Syria, as well as Egypt, Tunisia and Spain.
84f6b107-47b2-5cd1-a520-3a4f89856221.short_description: When the Caliph al-Walid ibn Abd al-Malik decided to build the first monumental mosque in Islamic history he used the most lavish material at his disposal and set the standard for subsequent religious monuments. Situated on top of an ancient sanctuary in old Damascus, the mosque has a courtyard, 122.5 x 50 m, surrounded by a colonnaded portico and a domed transept along the southern wall reminiscent of Byzantine churches. It was completed in AH 96 / AD 714–15 and some of its original marble panels and magnificent mosaics in blue, green and gold still survive along the western portico of the courtyard, particularly the 'Barada Panel'.
84f6b107-47b2-5cd1-a520-3a4f89856221.method_for_datation: The foundation inscription no longer exists but the text was preserved by the medieval Arab historian, traveller and geophrapher Ali ibn al-Husayn al-Mas'udi in his *Muruj al-dhahab wa-macadin al-djawhar \[Meadows of Gold and Treasury of Jewels*\], written in 332–45 / 943–56.

8789877a-2d27-5791-8029-f3833b2e3bfb.name: German “Jildirim Postcard”.
8789877a-2d27-5791-8029-f3833b2e3bfb.description: This photograph depicts a group of restrained men gathered beside railway tank wagons on the Hijaz railway network during the First World War. Although their precise identity cannot be established from the image alone, the visible chains indicate that they were under military or administrative custody. During the war, the Hijaz Railway and its connecting lines transported not only troops and military supplies, but also labour detachments, conscripts and detainees, revealing the railway's role as an instrument of wartime administration and control. For many inhabitants of Bilad al-Sham, the years of Safarbarlik (from the Ottoman Turkish seferberlik, meaning military mobilisation) were remembered as years of uncertainty and loss. Many families were separated by military service, others by compulsory labour or detention, while entire communities endured famine, displacement and social disruption. In local collective memory, Safarbarlik's presence in folk songs and stories embodies the human cost of the First World War, transforming an official term of mobilisation into a symbol of collective suffering for the region.

"

8a70de1b-8f52-5be5-84b2-f02ae35a3ab5.name: ‘Abd-al-Hamid (Abdülhamid) II (1842–1918)
8a70de1b-8f52-5be5-84b2-f02ae35a3ab5.short_description: Portrait of 'Abd-al-Hamid (Abdülhamid) II (1842–1918). He was born in 1842 in Istanbul. In 1876 he became Sultan and after the lost war with Russia in 1877, he was forced to agree to the 1878 Congress of Berlin. The signatory powers of the congress allowed Austria to occupy Bosnia-Herzegovina, which belonged to the territory of the Ottoman Empire. In 1888 he had to accept the occupation of Tunisia by France. He tried to modernize the Ottoman Empire with the help of Germany, but in 1908 a revolution of Turkish officers forced him to abdicate. He died in 1918 in Istanbul.

8c4076d1-62c9-5729-a3d5-d8c91345437b.name: Bridal headdress
8c4076d1-62c9-5729-a3d5-d8c91345437b.description: An example of coin-adorned accessories from Palestine dating to the early twentieth century, this bridal headdress originates from the villages of the Jaffa area. The coins incorporated into bridal ornaments symbolised part of the bride’s dowry, traditionally gifted by the groom’s family and considered her personal property, which she could keep and use according to her wishes. The embroidered motifs and techniques featured on the headdress are characteristic of the Jaffa region’s village dress traditions and are also found on women’s garments from the area.

8d173c69-e270-52ea-8792-452101a75d8b.name: Hospital (*Bimaristan*) Nur al-Din.
8d173c69-e270-52ea-8792-452101a75d8b.description:
The Bimaristan Nur al-Din, a hospital dating from the AH 6th / AD 12th century, is one of the most famous buildings in Damascus. At the time of its construction, it was considered remarkably new and refined, a sentiment recorded by the memoirs of the Valencian voyager from al-Andalus, Ibn Jubayr. It functioned as a therapeutic refuge for the sick as well as a medical school for aspiring physicians. The Mamluk Sultan Qalawun is said to have been saved from a lethal illness at this *bimaristan* – an experience which inspired him to build his famous institution in Cairo, The Complex of Sultan Qalawun. The Bimaristan Nur al-Din currently functions as a Museum of Arabic Medicine and Science. Located in a side road off the Suq al-Hamidiyyeh, it is easily discernable by its Mesopotamian-style red brick *muqarnas* dome rhythmically dotted with bulbs of dark glass. It is also famous for the eclecticism of its entrance façade, the woodcarving of its door, and the perfect balance of its axial symmetric four-*iwan* plan.  
The entrance block to the Bimaristan Nur al-Din protrudes at a right-angle to the building and it is accentuated by a portal featuring an unusually tall and shallow *muqarnas* façade, including a row of lobed arches at its base, and resting on top of a classically styled lintel. The door is an important example of fine wood carving and inlaid wood of the period. The identity of the door's designer is recorded in history as Abu al-Fadl Muhammad bin 'Abd al-Karim al-Harithi, known as al-Muhandis, or “the Geometer”. As both a medical doctor at the *bimaristan* and a creative craftsman of its gate, Abu al-Fadl demonstrates the multiplicity of expertise that scholars of this period usually enjoyed.  
The entrance leads into a square vestibule capped with a brick *muqarnas* dome; the adaptation of the *muqarnas* to the medium of stone was yet to take place in history. Once inside, the overhead *muqarnas* is a mesmerising vision of gradually receding cells pierced by beams of light.  
Passage through the vestibule leads to the grand rectangular courtyard and its central square basin with bracketed inner corners. Surrounding the courtyard are four arch-vaulted *iwan*s: the west *iwan* which leads to the entrance, the south and north *iwan*s on either side of the courtyard, and the main, east *iwan* which is larger than the others and faces the entrance. This main *iwan* represents the grand hall of the *bimaristan*, a place where students attended lectures by renowned physicians and had access to medical manuscripts for study. A marble dado rail with a *naskhi* inscription quotes passages from the Qur'an pertaining to medicine and healing. This serves as an allegory to the building's function as well as a holy blessing.  
Overlooking the southwest corner of the courtyard is an original arched window of perforated stucco, comprising a grid of octagonal stars with interlacing floral scrolls.
8d173c69-e270-52ea-8792-452101a75d8b.short_description: A charming survival of a medieval Syrian hospital, the *bimaristan* was built by Nur al-Din Mahmud bin Zangi in AH 549 / AD 1154. It had a strong architectural and institutional impact, inspiring the construction of Bimaristan al-Qaymari, also in Damascus, and the Sultan Qalawun complex in Cairo. The undulating *muqarnas* and classical-style lintel that accentuate its facade, the red-brick *muqarnas* dome and the perfect axial symmetry of the interior *iwans* around the courtyard, are examples of local adaptations to Eastern influences brought in by Nur al-Din. This *bimaristan* was a renowned medical centre in its timel.
8d173c69-e270-52ea-8792-452101a75d8b.method_for_datation: The monument is dated by the foundation text which is inscribed in four lineson a horseshoe-shaped marble sacramental table that is embedded in the eastern *iwan.*

8d429717-91c1-58a8-8960-902c72d886d5.name: Fluidity
8d429717-91c1-58a8-8960-902c72d886d5.description: Mohammed Al Saleem’s Fluidity can be used to evoke the landscape experience of travel across the Arabian Peninsula. Although the work does not directly depict the Hijaz Railway or a specific railway journey, its abstract treatment of horizon, light, movement, and space can be connected to the visual impressions encountered by travellers moving through desert landscapes. The painting may help viewers imagine the atmospheric experience of journeys in the region, including those historically associated with the Hijaz Railway. Rather than functioning as a documentary image, the work offers a modern artistic reflection on landscape, distance, and the fluid perception of space in motion.

8e570147-8f0e-58aa-a560-22e1e130385b.name: Le Boulevard El-Nassr, Damas (El-Nassr Boulevard, Damascus)
8e570147-8f0e-58aa-a560-22e1e130385b.description: Al Nasr Street in Damascus, previously known as Jamal Pasha Street, was renamed Al Nasr (Arabic: "Victory") in 1919. The street extends between the commercial centre near Suq al-Hamidiyya and the Hijaz Railway Station. Although an earlier route existed on the site, it was widened and monumentalized during the First World War under Jamal Pasha, the Military Governor of Ottoman Syria. The project formed part of a broader programme of urban transformation in the Ottoman provinces. The printed caption reads “Damas. — Le Boulevard El-Nassr un jour de fête,” ("Damascus—A Day of Celebration on El-Nassr Boulevard") and names the Damascus publishers Soubhi S. et Munir Aita. During this celebration, the street functioned as a gathering place on a scale that would have been difficult to accommodate within the narrow streets of Damascus's historic urban fabric. Soubhi and Munir Aita were photographers and imprint publishers active in Damascus, particularly during the 1920s.

8f578181-1de7-5276-b139-f1bfae497eec.name: Views of Syria
8f578181-1de7-5276-b139-f1bfae497eec.description: Collection of aerial views of historical monuments and cities of present-day Lebanon and Syria, taken approximately between 1925 and 1932 by the Jesuit missionary, explorer, and archaeologist Antoine Poidebard (1878–1955) and military pilots of the French Air Force. Considered the pioneer of aerial archaeology in the Middle East, Poidebard settled in Beirut in 1925 and was charged with mapping missions by the French mandatory authorities. With the logistical support of the French Air Force, he clocked up thousands of flying hours mainly above Lebanon and Syria, but also along the Mediterranean coast as far as Algeria and Tunisia. A highly talented amateur, he developed innovative technical processes and camera prototypes, paving the way for aerial archaeology as a scientific method.
8f578181-1de7-5276-b139-f1bfae497eec.author: Giulia Martini

8f8640bd-04ac-5181-ba28-bef663422bf2.name: *Panoramic View of Makkah - Arabia (West Asia). Panoramic View of Makkah during the Celebration of the Pilgrimage of the Muslims to the Kaaba, where the religious treasure is guarded*
8f8640bd-04ac-5181-ba28-bef663422bf2.short_description: This coloured print, perhaps from a late 19th-century, Spanish newspaper or magazine, shows a birds-eye view of the city of Makkah with the Holy Mosque and Ka'bah at the centre. The view was recorded from one of the rugged mountains surrounding the city. Hundreds of pilgrims are seen to approach from afar and converge on the city gates. that lead to the sanctuary. The print shows close compositional similarities to an early 19th century drawing by the English officer and artist Charles Hamilton Smith (1776-1859). Smith, although not known to have visited the Arabian peninsula, produced an album of drawings - possibly in turn taken from older engravings - with views from Syria, Persia and Arabia sometime between 1818 and 1846.

8fe00d65-80fb-5311-a2c8-55293c9c001c.name: Air France. Near East
8fe00d65-80fb-5311-a2c8-55293c9c001c.description: Travel poster advertising Air France flights to North Africa, depicting a Breguet 393T aircraft, a French three-engine airliner introduced in 1931 and operated by Air France on its Toulouse–Casablanca route, flying over figures in traditional dress, with a walled city and minaret in the background. Air France was founded in 1933 through the merger of five French airlines and rapidly built one of the most extensive international networks of its era, with North Africa among its earliest destinations. The poster was designed by Maurice Guiraud-Rivière (1881–1947), a French painter, draftsman, and sculptor born in Toulouse, whose Art Deco work frequently drew on themes of aviation, sport, and modernity.

912b204e-c92a-58e3-8cab-b04e1caa9f7e.name: Dome of the Rock.
912b204e-c92a-58e3-8cab-b04e1caa9f7e.description:
Dome of the Rock is one of the oldest Islamic monuments still standing today. It has a grandiose monumental form representing one of a small number of buildings in the Islamic world that may be chronicled as part of the creation and formation of an Islamic art in general.  
Dome of the Rock is built on an octagonal plan topped by a semi-circular great dome and supported by a circular drum. Four doors, each facing one of the cardinal directions, are built into the walls of the building. The façades are covered with marble panels at the bottom and ceramic (glazed) tiles at the top. These tiles date back to the time of Sultan Sulayman the Magnificent who ordered the replacement of the original glass mosaic with ceramic tiles in the period AH 952–9 / AD 1545–52. The marble panels were also renewed several times. The interior or inner drum, the cylinder which carries the dome, is also adorned with glass mosaic tiles. At present the outer dome is covered with gold-plated copper panels, although it was formerly of lead covered with a thin layer of gold-plate.  
Both the interior and exterior of the Dome of the Rock is built on an octagonal plan, surrounding the exalted Rock. According to Islamic belief the Rock is where the Prophet Muhammad ascended to the heavens (*Mi'raj*) on the night of his nocturnal journey from Mecca to Jerusalem *(Isra')*. The interior octagonal (which follows the outer octagon walls) is supported by eight piers and 16 columns. The rotunda is supported by four piers and 12 columns. Between the piers and columns span semi-circular arches, the façades and surfaces of which are decorated with mosaic tiles and colourful epigraphic texts. The rotunda is covered by a double dome. The inner dome has a diameter of 20.44 m, and is considered to be the oldest wooden structure still extant. It is composed of wooden panels that are decorated with written inscriptions and geometric decorations against a stucco background. Sixteen windows open on to the inside of the dome's drum. The drum is adorned with mosaic decorations and inscriptions from the Qur'an; it is enriched by a large number of inscriptions belonging to different restoration projects carried out by Muslim caliphs and sultans, the most famous being those that date to the Umayyad, Ayyubid, Mamluk and Ottoman periods. The dome is devoid of figurative decoration and exemplifies a response to changing religious orientation.
912b204e-c92a-58e3-8cab-b04e1caa9f7e.short_description: This is the jewel of Islamic architecture and the oldest Islamic monument that has not undergone fundamental changes. It thus provides very important testimony to the creation and formation of Islamic architecture and early Islamic decorative arts. It is also considered to be one of the most beautiful monuments in the world. The building is octagonal in form and is covered on the outside with marble and glazed tilework. The interior is decorated with marble, mosaics, plaster and wood. The great gold dome that towers over the building symbolises Jerusalem.
912b204e-c92a-58e3-8cab-b04e1caa9f7e.method_for_datation: The building is dated by a foundation inscription, written in the *kufic* script. Furthermore, there are a group of early Muslim historians such as al-Maqdisi al-Bishari, the famous geographer (who died at the end of the 4th / 10th century) and who dated the construction of the building to 72 / 691.

The most prominent among them being: the Fatimid caliph, al-Zahir (r. AH 411–27 / AD 1021–36), Sultan Salah al-Din Ayyubi (known as Saladin, r. AH 564–89 / AD 1169–93) and the Ottoman sultan, Sulayman the Magnificent (r. 926–74 / AD 1520–66).

91e561d2-6530-5965-bd21-e1a70b9ef590.name: Air France Brochure
91e561d2-6530-5965-bd21-e1a70b9ef590.description: This folding brochure, illustrated by an artist signing as Mariner, advertised Air France services to the Orient and the Far East for the summer of 1939. On its cover, the route runs from London and Paris to Marseille, divides as it crosses the Mediterranean and meets again in the Levant, before continuing to Baghdad and onwards to India, Southeast Asia and Hong Kong, a journey of eight days and more than 15,000 kilometres. A Dewoitine D-338 airliner, cut open to reveal its passengers, crew and cargo, promises comfort as well as speed. At the European end of the route stands a woman in an evening gown, while at the far eastern end another woman appears in East Asian dress. Inside, timetables, fares, visa regulations and currency tables guide the traveller across a map divided by colonial and mandate rule. Before the summer season was over, the outbreak of the Second World War disrupted this network of long-distance civilian air travel.
keywords: Advertisment; Travel; Flight; Art Deco; Holidays

93e8ae64-547f-5c2e-a1a2-19aee2c4d694.name: *Birkat al-Hajj*
93e8ae64-547f-5c2e-a1a2-19aee2c4d694.description:
The *Birkat al-Hajj*, the "pilgrimage’s reservoir", marks the most south-easterly extension of the Muslim city. The open, trapezoid-shaped reservoir measures 155 m x 122 m, edged by massive 3.5 m-thick walls of roughly hewn basalt-stone blocks. Three metre-wide projections divide the inner walls. The reservoir itself is between 6 m and 12 m deep. Stairs at the north-western, south-western and southeastern corners provide access to the water. The Birkat al-Hajj and another, slightly smaller, reservoir to the east secured the water supply for the city, collecting rain and melted ice from the Jabal Hauran and the Wadi al-Zaidi to the west of the city.  
  
In his description of Syria, the historian Ibn Shaddad al-Halabi mentions that the Ayyubid ruler of Damascus, al-Mu‘azzam ‘Isa (d. 624/1227), built a huge reservoir in the outskirts of Bosra, to serve as a drinking trough for the pilgrim’s caravan that passed on its annual journey to Mecca before entering the desert region. Describing his participation in the pilgrimage from Damascus in 726/1326, the traveller Ibn Battuta gives a vivid description of Bosra as pilgrim’s halt: “…we travelled on to the town of Bosra; it too is a small place. It is the usual practice of the caravan to stop there for four nights. The inhabitants of the Hauran flock to this town with their produce  
and the pilgrims supply themselves here with provisions for the journey.”  
  
The huge dimensions of the reservoir suggest that it must have provided water for a large city and not just for the  
pilgrims’ caravans that passed through twice a year. Therefore the initial structure may date to the Roman period (5th century AD) while the historically documented efforts of al-Mu‘azzam ‘Isa  
indicate a medieval renovation. This supposition matches very well with the extension of the citadel into a palatial residence for the lord of Bosra, the brother of al-Mu‘azzam, al-Salih Isma‘il,  
since the citadel with its newly constructed mosque and hammam required a sufficient and well-functioning water supply that the Birkat al-Hajj may well have provided.
93e8ae64-547f-5c2e-a1a2-19aee2c4d694.institution: Ministry of Culture, Directorate General of Museums and Antiquities
93e8ae64-547f-5c2e-a1a2-19aee2c4d694.author: Verena Daiber
keywords: Water; hydraulic system; Syria.

94c32a7d-017c-575e-a5ab-92b46e2819f5.name: A self-produced photocard showing a group of children and adults with travel snacks, waiting for a train
94c32a7d-017c-575e-a5ab-92b46e2819f5.description: A self-produced photocard showing a group of adults and children with provisions waiting for a train. Several heavily loaded camels stand behind the group, while baskets, bottles and other containers are carried by the people. A woman at the right holds a shallow basket containing what appears to be food. These provisions formed an important part of long-distance travel in the region. Before the railway, especially at Haj, caravans were used to transport travellers, merchandise and supplies southward, and merchants had their own camels to carry their loads toward Medina. After the railway, the use of animal transport remained important to move cargo and passengers to specific locations far from the stations.

94ef618f-769f-5a52-9aa5-25aac10e2373.name: London-Baghdad in 8 Days by Simplon-Orient-Express & Taurus-Express
94ef618f-769f-5a52-9aa5-25aac10e2373.description: Travel poster depicting the Arch of Ctesiphon (Taq Kasra) and advertising the passenger train route connecting London to Baghdad, operated by the "Compagnie Internationale des Wagons-Lits" (International Sleeping-Car Company). The journey combined two rail routes: the Simplon Orient Express from London to Istanbul, and the Taurus Express from Istanbul to Aleppo and Baghdad. Until 1935, the Syrian section terminated at Tel Kotchek, from where motor vehicles transferred passengers to Kirkuk; the final leg to Baghdad was by metre-gauge railway. The poster was issued by the French Paris-Lyon-Méditerranée (PLM) railway company and designed by French illustrator Roger Broders (1883–1953), best known for his Art Deco travel posters commissioned by the PLM, characterised by simple lines and bold, flat areas of colour.
94ef618f-769f-5a52-9aa5-25aac10e2373.author: Giulia Martini

9534f19d-962c-5eca-86f4-b14cd7c8f7af.name: Deutsches Soldaten u. Eisenbahnerheim in Eski-Chehir. Das Heim wurde 1916 eröffnet. (The Home of German Soldiers and Railway workers. The home was opened in 1916.
9534f19d-962c-5eca-86f4-b14cd7c8f7af.description: The Home of German Soldiers and Railwaymen (Deutsches Soldaten und Eisenbahnerheim) in Eskişehir opened in 1916. This institution served German military personnel and railway employees during the First World War. The building reflects the sizeable German railway community that had developed around Eskişehir after the town became an important junction of the German-backed Anatolian railway network. The Ottoman Anatolian Railway Company had already established a German Railway School beside Eskişehir station, operating since 1898 for the children of European railway officials and workers.

9599bee6-4ecd-5e61-803d-f6a17fddee21.name: The Istanbul Main Post Office
9599bee6-4ecd-5e61-803d-f6a17fddee21.short_description: The Istanbul Main Post Office is an office building for postal services located at Sirkeci quarter of Fatih district in Istanbul, Turkey. It was designed by architect Vedat Tek in First Turkish National architectural style and was constructed between 1903 and 1909. The four-story building houses a post office, the Sirkeci Post Office, office space for regional administration and also since 2000 the Istanbul Postal Museum. It is Turkey's largest post office building.

962c4a45-be4b-523c-a7fc-61da4af99fc5.name: Hijaz Railway Photograph Album

9a4260ca-f3e0-515c-9030-1c9a6bb50ae0.name: Oil Exploration
9a4260ca-f3e0-515c-9030-1c9a6bb50ae0.description: Abdullah Al Muharraqi’s Oil Exploration can be used to discuss Bahrain’s pioneering role in the oil history of the Gulf and the beginning of a wider regional transformation. Oil was discovered in Bahrain in 1932, making it the first country in the Arabian Gulf to enter the oil era. This discovery preceded similar turning points in neighbouring states, including Kuwait and Saudi Arabia in 1938, Qatar in 1939–1940, Abu Dhabi in 1958, and Oman in 1964. By showing workers around an oil well, the painting presents oil exploration not only as a technical or economic event, but also as a human and social process. The work is therefore useful for explaining how Bahrain’s early oil discovery marked the beginning of a new regional history, shifting Gulf societies from older economies based on pearling, maritime trade, and local labour toward oil-based modernisation, infrastructure, migration, and state formation.

9b7f13f5-9188-59a0-bf2d-8b4f7c9b66cb.name: Brass head of flagpole

The heads of flagstaffs were decorated with metallic items usually with Arabic calligraphy and some cosmic signs such as the crescent and the star.

9b9d3852-ed90-55a2-aeae-eba4ef451e30.name: Tomb of Joseph
9b9d3852-ed90-55a2-aeae-eba4ef451e30.description:
Folk tales differ with regard to the location of the Tomb of Joseph, with at least two potential places identified. The first is the Ibrahimi Mosque in Hebron (VIII.1.a), and the second is this location. Some historical sources mention that he was first buried in Nablus, and then moved to the Ibrahimi Mosque where a dome was built above his tomb. The site is venerated by the three monotheist religions due to Joseph’s distinct place in each of them.  
  
The shrine underwent reconstruction in 1868. It stands on top of an old well and consists of a square burial room that has a mihrab and which is covered by a dome. Nothing in the building indicates that any special attention was paid to it, possibly because most sultans paid more attention to the tomb in the Ibrahimi Mosque. The room is preceded by an open hall, which overlooks an open courtyard. Another small room is found to the west that was probably used by the attendant of the shrine.  
  
The edifice is in the local style that spread throughout the Ottoman period. The Ministry of the Waqf and Religious Affairs, which owns the site, has assigned the shaykh Fayad ‘Abd Allah family to look after it. The family has a document signed by the Ottoman Sultan ‘Abd al-Hamid that assigns them to serve and look after it.
9b9d3852-ed90-55a2-aeae-eba4ef451e30.author: Nazmi Al-Ju'beh
keywords: Nablus; funerary architecture; burial chamber; Palestine

9ca1f06f-1319-5325-a4ed-ef2842c72ef4.name: The Horse, the 50s spring
9ca1f06f-1319-5325-a4ed-ef2842c72ef4.description: Horses and camels were the traditional means of travel for nomadic and semi-nomadic groups in the Hijaz and Levant for generations. While the Hijaz Railway meant to industrialise the pilgrim travel from Damascus to Medina, quadrupeds remained an essential part of the pilgrimage route, as well as vital resources for the construction of the railway itself. While the railway served as a mechanised replacement for their labour, horses and camels remained vital to the path of the railway before, during and after its construction.

9cd33c79-f888-5848-ab0a-471109e32fbf.name: German military (propaganda) postcard (Feldpostkarte) published by F. Volckmar, Leipzig
9cd33c79-f888-5848-ab0a-471109e32fbf.description: Published in Leipzig by F. Volckmar as part of the German series Die Türkei im Weltkriege (Turkey in the World War), this field-postcard presents Jamal Pasha walking beside a train at a Damascus station with the figure described in its caption as the “Sharif of Mecca.” Ali Haydar Pasha, recognised as Sharif after Husayn ibn Ali by the Ottoman government, launched the Arab Revolt in 1916. Ali Haydar did not gain effective control of Mecca, making the title a political claim rather than an uncontested reality. Jamal Pasha, commander of the Ottoman Fourth Army and governor-general of the Syrian provinces during the war, was remembered locally as Jamal Pasha al Saffah “the blood-shedder” or “the butcher.” The name was associated particularly with his repression of Arab political activists and his order to execute prominent intellectuals, journalists and former officials after controversial wartime trials in Beirut and Damascus. The postcard was produced for a German audience, promoted an image of continued local loyalty to the Ottoman state and a unity within the German–Ottoman alliance, while concealing the conflict over control of the region and Hijaz.

keywords: Photography; military; Propaganda; War; World War

9f85fad2-9896-5d7d-84a8-ecc96ac39ee0.name: Picture  of Qasr al-Qatrane (here Catrané) on the Hijaz-Line with a basin for water-supply.
9f85fad2-9896-5d7d-84a8-ecc96ac39ee0.description: The large water basin at Qatraneh, identified in the French caption as Le grand Bassin à Catrané sur la ligne de Hydjaz. Behind it stands Qatraneh Fort, which was founded in 1531 under Sultan Süleyman I as part of a chain of fortified stopping places established to protect the pilgrimage caravan and secure water and supplies. Built of limestone and basalt, it has high crenellated walls, arrow slits and projecting machicolations, with rooms arranged around a narrow courtyard. Beside it lies the square reservoir, measuring about seventy metres on each side, used to collect seasonal runoff for travellers and animals. Once the Hijaz Railway followed the older pilgrimage corridor, Qatraneh became a railway station and the existing reservoir was reused as a water source. A 1906 report records that the shallow basin lost water through evaporation but remained valuable to railway construction and operation.

9ff5077e-cf93-5273-8105-87762d317700.name: *Ihram* belt
9ff5077e-cf93-5273-8105-87762d317700.short_description:
This *ihram* belt would have been worn by a male pilgrim, and used for carrying valuables while performing the Hajj rites. The *ihram* garment for men consists of two pieces of unstitched white cloth. One cloth (the *rida’*) is worn around the upper body while the other (the *izar*) would be worn wrapped around the lower body. This belt would have been worn around the waist on top of the *izar*. The inscription upon the belt wishes the wearer good health.  
As well as referring to ritual clothing, *ihram* also donates a state of mind in which a Muslim must enter in order to embark on Hajj. During this period, pilgrims must adhere to certain rules, for instance men and women are both forbidden from killing animals, uprooting trees, or cutting their nails or hair.

a16e766d-fa06-5cca-9cee-d7168a62177e.name: La Gare de Baramke, Damas (Baramkeh Station, Damascus)
a16e766d-fa06-5cca-9cee-d7168a62177e.description: Baramkeh Station, established in 1895 on the western side of Damascus, was a major passenger and freight station serving the Beirut–Damascus railway. A substantial railway complex, it contained warehouses for railway equipment, places for rent, two large yards with long platforms for loading and unloading goods, and a dedicated passenger area. It was an important gathering point for passengers travelling westward and to Beirut. Located in the Baramkeh district, in the northwestern part of a region previously known as Bustan al-Ahmar, the station was demolished during the urban redevelopment of Baramkeh in the late 1960s, and its site subsequently became an intercity bus terminal until 2007.

a3cbcd9b-cf11-5b68-9f33-19a8c46c9df8.name: Map of the Ottoman province (vilayet) of Damascus marking the Hijaz Railway line in red.
a3cbcd9b-cf11-5b68-9f33-19a8c46c9df8.description: The map is part of the Pocket Atlas of the Ottoman Lands: The Geographical and Statistical Conditions of the Ottoman State. It depicts the territories extending from the Hama region in the north through Damascus, the Hauran, and Jordan to the northern Hijaz. A red line begins at Hama and continues southward, representing the Hijaz Railway. A western branch extends toward the Mediterranean coast, corresponding to the railway connection between the main line and Haifa. The principal heading reads سوريه ولايتى, Vilayet of Syria. The vilayet was the principal provincial administrative unit established under the Ottoman provincial reforms of the nineteenth century. Vilayets were divided into sanjaks, and beneath the title the map identifies the four sanjaks of Damascus, Hama, Hauran, and Karak.
a3cbcd9b-cf11-5b68-9f33-19a8c46c9df8.bibliography: Masters, Bruce, *The Arabs of the Ottoman Empire, 1516–1918: A Social and Cultural History*, Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2013.

a43697f3-629f-54a0-ad35-dca00abfe608.name: Bau der Ḥiğâzbahn [graphic] : Schienenlegung bei Tebûk. 1906.
a43697f3-629f-54a0-ad35-dca00abfe608.alternate_name: Construction of the Hijaz railroad : Laying the rails near Tabuk. 1906 eng.
a43697f3-629f-54a0-ad35-dca00abfe608.description: This photograph entitled Bau der Ḥiğâzbahn [graphic] : Schienenlegung bei Tebûk. 1906 or Construction of the Hijaz railroad: Laying the rails near Tabuk. 1906 shows workers laying the rails near Tabuk as part of the Hijaz Railway. It is taken by Moritz Bernhard, and represents plate 56 in the portfolio: Bilder aus Palästina. Nord-Arabien und dem Sinai published in Berlin : Dietrich Riemer in 1916. a5573b67-ec0a-5821-8939-6d5d975f2b8a.name: London–Cairo in 7 Days by Train. Simplon-Orient-Express
a5573b67-ec0a-5821-8939-6d5d975f2b8a.description: Travel poster showing the silhouette of a woman carrying a pot on her head among palm trees by the Nile, with the pyramids in the distance, advertising the London–Cairo route via the Simplon Orient Express and its connecting services. Operated by the "Compagnie Internationale des Wagons-Lits" (International Sleeping-Car Company), the journey combined the Simplon Orient Express from London to Istanbul with onward rail, road and sea connections through Anatolia, the Levant and Palestine, reaching Cairo in approximately seven days. Designed by French illustrator Jacques Touchet (1887–1949), known for his work in magazine and book illustration, the poster dates to 1930.

a59d3d62-bb02-5cce-b693-cc1d841ab3e1.name: Damaskus (Bahnhof Kadem). (Damascus, Qadem Station)
a59d3d62-bb02-5cce-b693-cc1d841ab3e1.description: The postcard records the wider landscape surrounding the Qadam Station, on the urban edge of Damascus. The spacious compound with scattered service buildings and temporary tents shows that railway stations could extend beyond their passenger facilities and logistical zones. The open terrain surrounding the station reflects Qadam's position on the southern outskirts of Damascus, where sufficient land existed for railway expansion before the line continued towards the south and the Holy Cities. The coexistence of the station with its trains and the animal transportation outside of it demonstrates that modern rail infrastructure remained closely integrated with traditional patterns of mobility and movement. As the main southern operational station, Qadam formed the transition between the densely inhabited city of Damascus and the long open journeys towards Hijaz.

a650815a-4e3c-5270-8881-ef972e103baa.name: Suq of Khan al-Tujjar
a650815a-4e3c-5270-8881-ef972e103baa.description:
The location of the City of Nablus on the historical trade routes in Palestine had an enormous influence on boosting building activity there, which was funded by commercial revenue. A series of khans and wikalas were built during successive Islamic periods both inside and outside the city. However, all that remains of them today are a few intact examples and some ruins, in addition to some remaining fragments of their written history.  
  
The Suq of Khan al-Tujjar (also called Suq al-Sultani, the Sultan’s Market), as its name indicates, was the centre of economic and commercial life in Nablus. It was described in the records (sijils) of the Tribunal Court of Nablus and was also mentioned in the writings of Evlia Çelebi, a Turkish traveller who visited the city in 1082/1671–1672. Lala Mustafa Pasha, a Turkish minister and the wali of Syria (975/1567–979/1571), founded the suq and bestowed a waqf upon it. The suq is a large structure measuring 80 m. × 40 m.; two rows of shops are found on either side of a long lane. Its floor is made of beautiful flagstones, and it is covered by a series of high cross vaults, each of which is separated by pointed arches and pierced with skylights for ventilation. In the centre of the suq is a high dome that stands on a circular drum and has several openings for ventilation and light. Underneath it, and just in the centre of the shops to the south, lies a staircase that leads outside. Opposite, in the centre of the shops to the north, is an entrance that leads to Khan al-Tujjar, which the Turkish traveller Evlia Çelebi described as a fortress that had 150 adjacent rooms.  
  
The khan consists of two storeys: the first has open spaces that overlook the central courtyard, which was used in the past as stables but has now been turned into shops; the second storey is reached through a stone staircase that lies west of the courtyard. It consists of many rooms of different sizes that were used for guest accommodation. The rooms consist of three rows of domes preceded by three upper rooms from the west, east and south, which all overlook the central courtyard. Today they form the main road, or Suq al-Sagha (the Gold Market). Historical sources mention that there was a spring and a mosque that had a dome made of lead, the only one in Nablus, to the west of the khan. However, none of these structures has survived to the present as a result the earthquake that hit Nablus in 1345/1927, which also damaged the khan. Ihsan al-Nimr, the historian of modern Nablus, mentions that the second storey of the khan had a madrasa to teach the four schools of Islam, namely the Shafi‘i, Hanafi, Hanbali and Maliki.  
  
At the northern end of Suq al-Tujjar the remains of the Wikala al-Farrukhiyya can be seen. It was named after its founder the Amir Farrukh Ibn ‘Abd Allah al-Sharkasi in 1030/1620, a famous prince who ruled Jerusalem and Nablus and was appointed guardian of the pilgrimage (hajj) in Syria in the early 11th/17th century. Unfortunately nothing has survived of the building except for some rooms on its first and second floors, which are currently used as shops; the ruins are hardly representative of the place in its original form. As Ihasan al- Nimr mentions, the wikala hosted the Syrian pilgrimage caravan after it joined the Egyptian one in the south on the way to Hijaz.
keywords: Nablus; Suq; khan; wikala; caravanserai; trade routes; waqf; Hajj pilgrimage; Palestine

a6877d51-e0ec-5242-8b80-88d89c3d2ab4.name: Gare Chemin de fer Bagdad, Alep (Aleppo-Baghdad Railway Station)
a6877d51-e0ec-5242-8b80-88d89c3d2ab4.description: The postcard depicts Aleppo's Baghdad Railway Station, with the French description: Alep – Gare Chemin de fer Bagdad (Aleppo-Baghdad Railway Station), completed in 1912 as the northern Syrian terminus of the Baghdad Railway branch linking the city with Muslimiyeh station and the main line toward Mesopotamia. Situated in what became known as the Baghdad Station district, north of Aleppo's historic centre, the station was part of the development of a new modern quarter organised around transport and commerce. The station was constructed of stone masonry with broad overhanging roofs supported by timber brackets, pointed-arched openings and a monumental entrance pavilion. It was connected to the Baghdad Railway by a branch rather than the principal trunk line. The station became a strategic commercial gateway linking Aleppo with Anatolia in the north, and Mesopotamia as part of the wider Ottoman railway network.

a7473150-0733-5a34-b27e-a38c4f1684ce.name: Hijaz Railway Station
a7473150-0733-5a34-b27e-a38c4f1684ce.description:
The Hijaz Railway Station near Marjeh Square in central Damascus was conceived as the principal urban gateway to the railway connecting Damascus with Medina. Initiated in 1900 under Sultan Abdülhamid II and inaugurated in 1908, the Hijaz Railway sought to facilitate the pilgrimage to the holy cities while strengthening transport, communication and Ottoman administrative authority across the region.  
  
The monumental station building was designed by the Spanish architect Fernando de Aranda, who worked in Damascus during the late Ottoman period. Although railway services preceded its completion, the present building was finished around 1917. Its symmetrical façade, monumental entrance, distinctive arches and elaborate stone ornamentation combine the spatial organisation of European railway terminals with architectural forms inspired by the local historic buildings of Damascus. Inside, a spacious entrance hall, richly decorated wooden ceilings and coloured glass reflect the craftsmanship of local artisans and the architectural implementation of the period.  
  
Beyond its practical function, the station represented a transformation in the relationship between Damascus and the wider region. It became a point of departure and arrival for pilgrims, travellers and goods, while its position within the expanding modern city connected railway infrastructure with new streets and public spaces. Following the disruption of the Hijaz Railway during the First World War, the building remained an important landmark of Damascus, preserving the memory of a railway that shaped the region’s travel, connections and cultural exchange.

Below, the timetable promises that a letter posted on Saturday morning would reach Naples the same afternoon, Athens on Sunday and Beirut on Monday. An arrow beyond Beirut points further east, towards the routes the company would soon open.

a8ba1fa9-babe-58f8-a236-0758c7c190cc.name: A self-produced photocard showing a small typical Ottoman railway station
a8ba1fa9-babe-58f8-a236-0758c7c190cc.description: This postcard shows Beirut Railway Station on the Beirut–Damascus railway, Beirut. With around 140,000 inhabitants in the early 1860s, Beirut was the region's major port and commercial centre, while Damascus, with nearly 200,000 inhabitants, functioned as the provincial capital and an important market for many products. Before the railway, Beirut and Damascus were connected by a 108-km mule road not suitable for caravans; archives note that the journey took approximately four days. The railway concession was granted in 1891, and the 147 km Beirut–Damascus railway opened in 1895. An Ottoman timetable reproduced from the official Suriye Vilâyeti Salnâmesi (Annual of the Province of Syria) records two daily departures from Beirut, at 07:05 and 17:30, on a route comprising between twenty-five and thirty stops.

aa4878d5-82c1-50ac-a798-91386bc0bd59.name: Maan Station, Hedjaz R.R. [i.e., Hejaz Railroad]
aa4878d5-82c1-50ac-a798-91386bc0bd59.description: This photograph of Maʿan station, preserved as a glass negative in the G. Eric and Edith Matson Photograph Collection at the Library of Congress, was produced by the American Colony Photo Department or its successor, the Matson Photo Service. One of 22000 photographs in the collection, it depicts a part of the railway beside a stone station building, with a pitched roof. The station served the Hijaz Railway in present-day Jordan, with the Damascus–Maʿan section opening in 1904. Long before the railway’s construction, Maʿan was an important stop on the Hajj caravan route and a frontier town between Syria and the Hijaz. Its pilgrimage fair contributed to its prosperity during the nineteenth century, as reflected in the accounts of Georg August Wallin, who visited in 1845 and 1848. During the Arab Revolt, the station and its surrounding defences became a focus of fighting, as recorded by T. E. Lawrence.

aaabc192-01bc-59ee-bc6c-ebd3ae07bab2.name: Station de Hijaz, Damas (The Hijaz Station, Damascus)
aaabc192-01bc-59ee-bc6c-ebd3ae07bab2.description: The Hijaz Railway Station is located on the western side of the Old City of Damascus, west of Bab al Nasr, near the entrance to Souq al Hamidiyah. It is situated at the intersection of al Nasr Street, Saadallah al Jabiri leading to al Halbouni area, and Muslim al Baroudi Street, which leads towards the Baramkeh district. The site where the station was built had previously served as the gathering place for pilgrims arriving from across Asia. Pilgrims assembled in Damascus before departing in a ceremonial caravan led by the Ottoman Governor of Damascus. The procession followed a route through the Midan district toward Qadam and continuing south toward the Hijaz.

ac213e50-9aa9-50fe-a88f-16a3840fbce1.name: *Departure of a Caravan to Mecca from Bab el-Nasr Gate, Cairo*
ac213e50-9aa9-50fe-a88f-16a3840fbce1.short_description: Traditionally, most Muslim pilgrims went to Makkah on foot as part of a caravan. Cairo was one of the most important starting points for pilgrim caravans, particularly as it dispatched the ceremonial Mahmal, an ornamental litter containing a Qur’an manuscript and ritual hangings for the Holy Places. Traditionally, the Hajj caravan left the city from the Bab al Nasr gate. In order to ensure the caravan's smooth progression, the Amir al-Hajj organised each section and allocated it its correct place within the sequence. The caravan was headed up by bedouin guides, followed by water carriers and important officials. Next came the treasury and precious gifts intended for the Holy Places, carefully shielded by the ruler's special guards and soldiers. Another, well-protected treasury section - this one intended for the upkeep of the caravan itself - followed and, behind it, a numerous array of traders and merchants. The rest of the caravan was made up of the actual pilgrims from all over the region.

ad6aaf4a-2118-5025-a77a-00c66b5583c0.name: Jildrim postcard
ad6aaf4a-2118-5025-a77a-00c66b5583c0.description: This photographic postcard records a group of travellers gathered in and beside an open railway wagon during the First World War. During the war, the Hijaz Railway and its connected lines became military supply routes. They moved soldiers, labourers, food, weapons, timber, animals and construction material toward Palestine and Sinai. Wartime expansion increased the pressure on locomotives and rolling stock already limited in number. The vehicle was built for goods, yet contemporary railway reports show that freight wagons were also used to move large groups of people when passenger coaches were insufficient, especially during military mobilisation.

ae99c07a-63eb-5689-9082-49c9d484164e.name: *Suq al-Hamidiyya, Damascus*
ae99c07a-63eb-5689-9082-49c9d484164e.short_description: The Suq al-Hamidiyya, built in 1886 and 1894, is by far the biggest and most famous suq in Damascus. This bazaar street also links the two most important historic buildings, the Umayyad Mosque and the Citadel. It was built along its western section by incorporating earlier structures, whereas the eastern part of the street was a completely new construction cutting through the existing buildings. The commercial thoroughfare is 450 metres long and 8.70 to 9.90 metres wide, its enormous size and the high standard of its execution accentuate new design principles. So in various respects, this suq is a very interesting example of structural change in a traditional commercial centre.

b09beb3b-1d0b-53ab-b342-7ea606b4ebe1.name: Mudawwara
b09beb3b-1d0b-53ab-b342-7ea606b4ebe1.description:
The last station before entering Saudi borders on the Pilgrimage route, the complex at Mudawwara comprises a fortress, a water reservoir, and a paved road.  
The fortress has a square plan (19 m x 19 m). The maximum preserved height is about 9 m. The whole structure was built of sandstone blocks. From the outside the fortress was articulated by small towers at the upper corners, while the corners at the ground level were strengthened by buttresses at about 1 m from the ground. The walls were provided with two rows of slit windows. The tops of the northern and western walls were flat while the eastern and southern walls were decorated with battlements. It is noteworthy in this regard that the northern and western walls are slightly higher than the two other walls and their tops are of different masonry; most probably they were built in later periods.  
The gate complex is located at the centre of the eastern wall. It consists of a rectangular entrance and a barrel-vaulted passageway leading to the central courtyard (about 8 m x 8 m). The entrance is marked by a large (about 5.5 m x 2.5 m) machicolation (projecting window), comprising one large window with two slit windows either side, resting on an arch supported by corbels. At ground level nine barrel-vaulted rooms were organised around the central courtyard. The staircases to the first floor were placed on both sides of the passageway. On the first floor nine rooms of different sizes and shapes were built around a central courtyard.
b09beb3b-1d0b-53ab-b342-7ea606b4ebe1.short_description: The last Jordanian station on the Pilgrimage route to Hijaz, the complex at Mudawwara comprises a fortress, a reservoir and a paved road. The fortress, dated to the time of Abdullah Pasha (Governor of Damascus AH 1142–5 / AD 1730 –3), is built of sandstone blocks with a square plan (19 m x19 m). The walls were provided with two rows of slit windows. The tops of the northern and western walls were flat while the eastern and southern walls, shorter and perhaps earlier, were decorated with battlements. The entrance is marked by a large projecting window on an arch supported by corbels.
b09beb3b-1d0b-53ab-b342-7ea606b4ebe1.method_for_datation: On the basis of historical documents the fortress was dated to the time of Abdullah Pasha, Governor of Damascus from 1730 to 1733. Stylistic analysis suggests that at ground level the rooms are arranged around a central courtyard, Peterson (1986) attributed Mudawwara and Hasa to the early 12th / 18th century.

b4a14dd7-63bc-5f3a-b31a-2ae6a297fc74.name: Qatranah Railway Station
b4a14dd7-63bc-5f3a-b31a-2ae6a297fc74.short_description: Qatranah is an important station on the Hijaz railway. It consists of a group of building along the railroad. The station had been protected by a renovated small 16th-century fortress located to the west of the railway. The fortress was provided with water wells and pools for both the humans and the animals. The various components of the project including the rails, steam engines, bridges, stations were an industrial, architectural and engineering statement that had a huge influence on Jordan. The tracks and the station was completed in September 1904.
b4a14dd7-63bc-5f3a-b31a-2ae6a297fc74.history: In 1900-1908, Sultan Abdul Hamid with the help and support of Germany established a Railway between Damascus and Mecca (1700 km) to facilitate transporting the pilgrims. The track from Medina to Mecca (400 km) was never realized. The cost of the project was estimated at approximately 5 million Ottoman golden liras, which were provided from: private donations, revenues of the Ottoman State from the sale of stamps, and a special tax upon all citizens for the railway. Construction of the narrow-gauge track (105cm) began in 1900 with a wire telegraph line along its side connecting Damascus with Medina across Amman with a total track length of 1303 km. Official inaugurations of the tracks and stations were scheduled to coincide with the accession of the Sultan to the throne in the month of September every year. The construction of the project ended in 1908.

b6eaa68e-89bb-5d41-9802-1508be85c8ac.name: Mausoleum of Saladin (Salah al-Din).
b6eaa68e-89bb-5d41-9802-1508be85c8ac.description:
Salah al-Din's (Saladin's) tomb is located next to the northwestern corner of the Great Umayyad Mosque. Although Saladin died in AH 589 / AD 1193, he was initially interred at the Damascus Citadel until his son al-Malik al-Afdal Nur al-Din 'Ali, ruler of Damascus, completed the construction of the mausoleum. Saladin's body was transferred to its final resting place on the holy day of 'Ashura in AH 592 (AD 1195). Soon afterwards, Salah al-Din's other son, al-Malik al-Aziz ‘Uthman (‘Uthman II), ruler of Egypt, decided to construct a *madrasa* attached to his father's tomb. Thus it is also known as al-Madrasa al-'Aziziyya. The events surrounding the death and burial of Saladin are clearly recorded in the historical sources, based on the eyewitness account of Imad al-Din al-Isfahani (d. AH 597 / AD 1201), who was Saladin's confidant and administrative genius.  
The construction of the tomb is typically Damascene: a square chamber with *ablaq* walls and four arches capped by a cupola. The movement from square room to circular dome is achieved by a transitional drum in two zones: octagonal and 16-sided polygonal. The interior of the tomb chamber is mounted with blue and green Ottoman tiles of the AH 11th / AD 17th century known as *qashani*. More subtle decoration can be seen in the stone-paste floral and geometric designs above the arches.  
In the middle of this domed chamber lie two coffins. The white marble coffin was a gift from the German Emperor William II on the occasion of his visit to Damascus in 1903. Next to it is the original wooden cenotaph, a masterpiece of the linear interplay typical of Ayyubid woodworking. It is decorated with geometric and astral patterns as well as floral and vegetal motifs.  
The tomb chamber occupies the southwest corner of the building. A chamber used for Qur'anic recitation is accessible from its east side and a series of five smaller rooms are found along the north side. As for the building's exterior and its connection to the Madrasa Aziziyya, little of this original architecture has survived to modern times.
b6eaa68e-89bb-5d41-9802-1508be85c8ac.short_description: Saladin's tomb is located in close proximity to the Great Umayyad Mosque and is considered a holy site. His mausoleum was built by his sons after his death in AH 589/ AD 1193 and his body was transferred there in 592 / 1195. The architecture is typically Damascene Ayyubid: a square chamber decorated with alternating muti-coloured stones and capped by a dome. The coffin itself is a very important example of the art of Ayyubid woodcarving. A second coffin, made of white marble, was presented as a gift to Damascus by the German Emperor in 1903.
b6eaa68e-89bb-5d41-9802-1508be85c8ac.method_for_datation: The original inscriptions have been modernised, but contemporary Ayyubid histories contain accounts of Salah al-Din's burial. Stylistic comparisons of Damascene Ayyubid architecture also support the 6th- / 12th-century dating.

b705e8a3-17fc-5217-8640-d86017b77c66.name: Zamzam Water Bottle
b705e8a3-17fc-5217-8640-d86017b77c66.short_description: This simple, circular Zamzam bottle has been constructed from copper-alloy sheet and decorated with hammered and incised decoration. A very narrow cylindrical neck gives access to the body of the vessel, and a chain secured to its shoulder allows it to be carried. Every pilgrim to the Holy City of Makkah will make a point of drinking and collecting water from the sacred well of Zamzam, located near the Ka’bah within the precinct of the Holy Mosque at Makkah al Mukarramah. Its never ceasing flow is considered a miracle, and its properties are believed to aid good health and wellbeing. To this day, pilgrims to Makkah make a point of taking as much Zamzam water as they can back with them, not least to distribute it to loved ones and treasured friends in order to allow them to partake in the water's beneficial properties.

b736daf3-734c-59a9-b14b-65272a0a6bc9.name: Stereoview entitled ‘*The Holy Carpet Parade, Cairo, Egypt- Starting for Mecca*’
b736daf3-734c-59a9-b14b-65272a0a6bc9.short_description: This very early photograph of the Mahmal ceremony, printed as a stereograph, shows the Mahmal parading through a narrow Cairene street amongst a thronging crowd; some bystanders have their arms outstretched in prayer. Behind travels a retinue of officials carrying banners, as the caravan leaves for pilgrimage. It was published by an American company based in Washington named J.F Jarvis, one of a small number of stereograph producers in the late 19th century. Jarvis began as a photographer using his own photographs to create stereographic views and later began publishing scenes from all over the world. This stereograph was sold by Underwood & Underwood. Founded in 1881 the company was known as the largest distributer of stereographs in the world until 1920, when it was sold to the Keystone View Company. Many of Underwood & Underwood’s stereographs depicted regions in the Middle East, covering landscapes and historical sites. This type of view may have originally been sold as part of a boxed set, together with other views of Egypt.

b968650a-b220-5bfb-b654-c97f12ec1056.name: Map of the Ottoman district (mutasariflik) of Jerusalem.
b968650a-b220-5bfb-b654-c97f12ec1056.description: The Mutasarrifate of Jerusalem was a late-Ottoman administrative district governed directly from Istanbul; it was not part of the neighbouring vilayets of Beirut or Syria. Listed on the map are its four subordinate kazas: Yafa, Bir al-Sabea, Gaza, and Khalil al-Rahman. The red line crossing the map between Yafa on the Mediterranean coast and Jerusalem represents the Yafa–Jerusalem Railway. Initiated by the Jerusalemite Ottoman entrepreneur Yosef Navon, its concession was transferred to French investors and the line was operated by the Société du Chemin de Fer Ottoman de Jaffa à Jérusalem et Prolongements. The railway line opened in 1892; it was an approximately 87-km narrow-gauge line through the coastal plain, via Lydda and Ramla, before climbing through the hills toward Jerusalem.

ba590c72-051f-5d9a-898f-073b4347852b.name: *Port, Beirut*
ba590c72-051f-5d9a-898f-073b4347852b.short_description: On 19/6/1887, the Ottoman authority gave the concession of the Port to an Ottoman company under the name of "Compagnie du Port, des Quais et des Entrepôts de Beyrouth". The concession was later fortified when the company gained from the Customs the sole rights to store and carry all the transit goods passing through the Customs. Constructions works namely a maritime dam to expand and develop the Port were accomplished and the opening on the occasion of the accomplishment of these works was celebrated by the end of 1894, basins were developed and spread between Ras Al Shamiah and Ras Al Mudawar. It forms the midpoint of three continents: Europe, Asia and Africa, which makes the Port a passage for ship fleets between East and West. During the mid 70's, the Port of Beirut was an important international trading station with the surrounding Arab countries and up until today it has preserved its commercial nature.

ba660d1c-5f38-5a9c-90c6-7a2cf5e424f9.name: Bau der Bagdadbahn (Baghdad Building)
ba660d1c-5f38-5a9c-90c6-7a2cf5e424f9.description: The Baghdad Railway was one of the largest railway projects in the late Ottoman Empire. The line was conceived as a continuation of the Anatolian railway system from Konya across southern Anatolia toward Baghdad. In 1903, a concession was made to the Imperial Ottoman Baghdad Railway Company, which planned to cross the Taurus Mountains, descend toward the Adana–Mersin line, and continue through Aleppo toward Mesopotamia. The mountainous sections created major engineering and financial difficulties. While the first 200 km from Konya to Bulgurlu opened in 1904, further construction slowed considerably, particularly because crossing the Taurus range required extensive tunnels, bridges and other infrastructure. The Baghdad Railway remained incomplete until 1940. The First World War interrupted the construction, and the dissolution of the Ottoman Empire left the project unfinished. The final section connecting the railway to Baghdad was later constructed by the Iraqi State between 1936 and 1940.

bd41700c-08db-55d1-89a5-2d1602e75424.name: Welcoming Captives of Abdulhamid after the Constitution
bd41700c-08db-55d1-89a5-2d1602e75424.description: Beirut Port Station was a public gathering place during the political transformation of 1908. Its bilingual caption, “Welcoming Captives of Abdulhamid after the Constitution / Des emprisonnés bien accueillis de Abdulhamid après la Constitution,” identifies the crowd as welcoming prisoners associated with the rule of Sultan Abdülhamid II after the restoration of constitutional government. Abdülhamid II restored the Ottoman constitution and reconvened parliament after the Young Turk Revolution of July 1908, and it was accompanied by the release of political prisoners and exiles. Locally, there was relative public support for the constitutional revolution among sections of Beirut's intellectual and mercantile population.

bd511092-0183-5780-8a32-1842a109f127.name: Pictures from Palestine, Northern Arabia and the Sinai
bd511092-0183-5780-8a32-1842a109f127.description: Photographic account showing major sites and geographic features of Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Syria, Egypt, and Palestine. Pictures depict pilgrims on the Hajj to Mecca, Bedouins, the construction of the Hijaz Railway between Damascus and Medina, and views of Jeddah, Petra, and Mount Sinai. Most of the photographs were taken between 1905 and 1915 by Bernhard Moritz (1859–1939), a German Orientalist, Arabist, and archaeologist, but some also by his Turkish colleagues, especially for areas where non-Muslims were prohibited from going. From 1896 to 1911, Moritz headed the Khedival Library and Archive in Cairo, from where he conducted numerous research trips to the Sinai and Hijaz.

bd5974b2-add3-5352-9473-20bfa7b6d015.name: Beiteddine Palace
bd5974b2-add3-5352-9473-20bfa7b6d015.description: The construction of the palace took ten years. Celebrated Lebanese constructors, such as Rustam and Yusuf Mujahes from Shuwayr were employed, as well as a number of European engineers and architects invited by the Prince Bashir al-Shihabi. Tiles were also imported from celebrated masters in Istanbul, Aleppo and Damascus.
bd5974b2-add3-5352-9473-20bfa7b6d015.history:
A tile framework imported from Marseille was added to this palace at the beginning of Prince Bashir al-Shihabi's reign resembling the typical Lebanese house, a future national symbol. The palace is interesting, as the ornamentation shows clear influences from the late Ottoman architecture, whereas the façade contains more neoclassical (or late baroque) elements from the late 19th and early 20th centuries. These additions did not alter the basic structure of the building, however. Ways the structure of this palace differed notably from the traditional models include: the location of a central stair inside the main hall, rather than outside, and the transformation of the patio into a public space between the palace and the street.  
Beiteddine palace was built to replace the palace at Deir al-Qamar, which had become too small for the expanding number of soldiers and servants. The prince ordered a luxurious palace to be built on the hill overlooking Deir al-Qamar, on land he had bought upon his marriage to "Sitt al-Shams.”

bd854006-fb1c-530f-bea4-1bc64cf1ec02.name: A Bedouin sits on the old iron track of the Hejaz Railway in Saudi Arabia
bd854006-fb1c-530f-bea4-1bc64cf1ec02.description: The Hijaz Railway was a political and social endeavour as well as a religious enterprise to benefit the Islamic world, but the railway line was also a great feat of construction and engineering. Much of the construction took place over immensely hostile and rugged terrain under challenging conditions; given the scarcity of water and extreme heat, it was undoubtedly an extraordinary achievement.

bea26544-aced-52fd-b07c-079721229f74.name: Suq al-Qattanin (Market of the Cotton Merchants).
bea26544-aced-52fd-b07c-079721229f74.description:
The Suq al-Qattanin extends from east to west measuring approximately 95 m. This commercial *suq* contains a *caravanserai*, two *hammams*, and two rows of 30 shops, totalling 60 shops in all. The *suq* is designed on a rectangular plan, and has a ceiling that is arched with a barrel-shaped vault divided into a series of arches totalling 30 sections. Each section opens up into a skylight to allow light and air into the interior. The *suq* was built of white dressed stone that has turned ashen grey over time. Each shop has a wooden door.  
The *suq* has two entrances, one on the east and the other on the west. The east entrance is called Bab al-Qattanin (Gate of the Cotton Merchants), which opens on to the west side of the Haram. This entrance was built with meticulous care and is considered an architectural rarity. The entrance consists of a recess with a tri-lobed arch, encircled by another large recess. This recess is crowned by a tapered arch and topped by a semi-dome that is supported by five tiers of stone *muqarnas*. The entrance was built from black, grey and red stone and arranged with meticulous attention in the *ablaq* style, whose correspondence of colour is well known in the Islamic architecture of Jerusalem, especially in those buildings that date to the Mamluk period.  
The west entrance to the *suq* is simpler in both design and architectural composition and consists of a rectangular portal, above which is a large lintel. The lintel consists of seven joggled stones, on top of which rests a relieving arch. A circular window opens out above it. The elements of this entrance are located within a recessed wall surrounded by a large pointed arch.  
The Suq al-Qattanin is considered to be one of the most complete and beautiful *suqs* not only in Palestine, but in the whole of Bilad al-Sham (Greater Syria). Income from the *suq* was allocated to the Haram al-Sharif, and towards projects in Jerusalem undertaken by Amir Tankaz al-Nasiri, such as the Madrasa Tankaziyya.
bea26544-aced-52fd-b07c-079721229f74.short_description: This suq is the most beautiful market in the city. It has not undergone fundamental changes since it was built. The *suq* is characterised by a rectangular market hall approximately 95 m long. It is surrounded on two sides by two rows of shops, 60 in total, in addition to a *khan* (inn) and two bathhouses. On the east side of the suq an imposing portal, considered to be one of the most beautiful Mamluk monuments in the city, opens onto the west side of al-Haram al-Sharif.
bea26544-aced-52fd-b07c-079721229f74.method_for_datation: The *suq* is dated by three written foundational inscriptions, and supported by the writing of the historian, Mujir al-Din al-Hanbali (d. 928 / 1521).

c0a299b6-5820-525a-a042-a0c808c72430.name: Citadel of Jerusalem.
c0a299b6-5820-525a-a042-a0c808c72430.description:
The Citadel of Jerusalem contains a great outer wall, a moat, five towers, a principle eastern portal, several open courtyards, two mosques and a minaret. It assumed its present form during the Ottoman era, although this was the result of an architectural development that began in the Greco-Roman period and which developed over time to its present state. The fortress or citadel, and the principle tower in it (known widely as the Tower of David) were destroyed in AH 637 / AD 1239 so that it would not fall into the hands of the Crusaders. Several attempts were made by Sultan Nasir Muhammad Ibn Qalawun in AH 710 / AD 1310 to rebuild it. This was followed by a comprehensive project to restore the fortress during the reign of Sultan Sulayman the Magnificent in AH 938 / AD 1531; this included enclosing the citadel with battlements.  
The citadel is considered to be one of the major landmarks of Jerusalem, for it links the walls of the old city and encompasses the city's most important buildings, such as the Aqsa Mosque, the Dome of the Rock, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and the Wall of al-Buraq. The great traveller, Awliya' Chalabi (Evliya Çelebi in Turkish) described the citadel when he visited Jerusalem in AH 1059 / AD 1649 extolling both its strategic and administrative importance during the Ottoman period. Besides being the first comprehensive restoration programme to be undertaken by the Ottoman Sultanate in Jerusalem, the citadel was also where the Janissary army resided.  
The plan of the citadel is an irregular rectangle: three sides of it are almost straight while the fourth, south wall zigzags following the old line of the original fortification, which was itself dictated by the south-sloping topography of the site. The citadel is encompassed within an outer curtain wall that was built with huge stone blocks, seen especially in the foundations and the lower courses.  
The citadel is defended by five large towers, four of which are set at the corners of the citadel, while the fifth is at the centre of the eastern wall in the middle of an open courtyard. The citadel is surrounded by a moat that is clearly visible from inside the city on the north and east sides.  
The interior of the citadel is accessed by means of the principle, eastern portal which is composed of two sections or gates. The first, outer gate has a double staircase, the landing of which can be reached from both the north and the south. The second interior gate is placed within a receding niche crowned by a pointed arch. On the outside of the arch there is an inscription which states that the renovation of the citadel took place in AH 938 / AD 1531–2 by order of Sultan Sulayman. The outer entrance is separated from the inner portal by a fixed wooden bridge. To the left (south) of the bridge there is an open-air mosque for use in the summer months. Worked into the front fortifications is the *tughra* of Sultan Sulayman.
c0a299b6-5820-525a-a042-a0c808c72430.short_description: The solitary Citadel of Jerusalem is located at the centre of the Western Wall of the city. It is a large complex which contains a variety of defensive features: a large outer wall, a trench, a drawbridge, five towers, an eastern principle entrance, a number of open plazas, two mosques and a minaret. These buildings were a result of defensive works dating from the  time of the Romans until the Ottoman period. In its present form its core dates to the Mamluk and Ottoman periods.
c0a299b6-5820-525a-a042-a0c808c72430.dates: The citadel dates to hegira the 8th / AD 14th century and to the AH 10th / AD 16th century. In the citadel there are remains from the 1st century BC to the AH 6th / AD 12th century.
c0a299b6-5820-525a-a042-a0c808c72430.method_for_datation: The dating of the citadel and its various sections depended upon several Ayyubid, Mamluk and Ottoman inscriptions, some of which are still *in situ*. Ceramic fragments and architectural remains recovered in archaeological excavations have also helped to decide an accurate dating.

c23ab188-f83e-57b5-8232-5889cabef0e8.name: Dinar
c23ab188-f83e-57b5-8232-5889cabef0e8.description: This half-dinar note was issued by the Government of Iraq around 1942, under a currency law passed in 1931. Its portrait shows King Faisal II as a small child, for he had come to the throne in 1939 at the age of three. The note was engraved and printed in England by Bradbury, Wilkinson & Co., and its reverse, written entirely in English, explains that it could be exchanged for sterling. Although Iraq had been formally independent since 1932, its money was still managed through a currency board chaired from London, and the country had only just emerged from a brief war with Britain in 1941, after a nationalist coup.
keywords: Iraq; Money; Bill; Faisal II; King

c25e83e8-79d8-5ca2-95b2-2a9dca7ab11e.name: Mekleb bridal ornament
c25e83e8-79d8-5ca2-95b2-2a9dca7ab11e.description: Dating to approximately 1900, this exquisite Mekleb ornament worn on the back of the bride serves as both a significant ceremonial adornment and a powerful protective token. The piece is richly embellished with an array of historical coins, traditional amulets, and vibrant glass beads. Notably, the prominent blue-colored elements integrated into the ornament function as protective amulets, culturally intended to shield the bride from the evil eye and envy.

c2cc2d61-09ed-5140-86b6-7a7bc1706b32.name: Conversation with Nasser at the Royal Palace of Dedinje, Belgrade
c2cc2d61-09ed-5140-86b6-7a7bc1706b32.description: Josip Broz Tito and Gamal Abdel Nasser are shown in conversation at the Royal Palace of Dedinje in Belgrade on 16 July 1956, during Nasser's state visit to Yugoslavia. The two leaders, both in military uniform, appear relaxed and engaged, an image that also hints at their shared background as soldiers who became heads of state. The meeting came at a decisive moment in the search for a political alternative to the Cold War blocs. Two days later, Tito, Nasser and Indian Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru met on the Brioni Islands, where, on 19 July, they issued a joint statement articulating principles that would later become central to the Non-Aligned Movement, formally launched at the Belgrade Conference in 1961 with the participation of 25 countries. The photograph captures a moment in the deepening relationship between Yugoslavia and Egypt, at a time when states across Asia, Africa and beyond were seeking greater autonomy from the dominant Cold War blocs.

d0602307-9a81-587d-b9b3-2b8e93c844eb.short_description: The station is rectangular in shape with a length of about 700 meters and a width of about 150 meters, and is surrounded by a fence built of black basalt stone, and comprises a set of 11 buildings including the main one. d0602307-9a81-587d-b9b3-2b8e93c844eb.history:
The Hijaz railway was very important for the Islamic world where pilgrims could reach al-Hijaz safe and in short time comparing to what was before. The station was known in al-Madina as *istasyon*, a Turkish word meaning station.  
The station is located west of the Prophet 's Mohammed (PBU) Mosque and approximately 1 km a way, in the region now known Aanbariyah beside Anbariyah Mosque and Alanbariyah Gate, which was removed for the purpose of expanding the streets in the area.  
The first train arrived to al-Madina in 23rd of August 1908 and the official ceremony for the opening of the Station was held a week later.

d0a848cc-445a-5603-a7fc-832f779a1817.name: Postcard of “Mecca-Pilger in der Eisenbahn, Jerusalem“. (Mecca-Pilgrims on the Railway)
d0a848cc-445a-5603-a7fc-832f779a1817.description: The photograph shows three passengers through the open windows of a wooden railway carriage on their journey to the annual Hajj, one of the largest recurrent pilgrimage movements of people in the Islamic world. Before the construction of the Hijaz Railway, pilgrims travelling toward the Holy Cities usually spent several weeks crossing many regions by walking and camel caravans. The opening of the railway between 1900 and 1908 reduced this journey to only a few days, making the pilgrimage faster, safer and more accessible for many travellers. At the same time, railway travel transformed the social experience of the pilgrimage. Shared railway carriages brought together pilgrims from different provinces, languages and social backgrounds, replacing much of the traditional rhythm of caravan travel with a new form of collective mobility that reflected the technological and administrative reforms in the late Ottoman period.
d0a848cc-445a-5603-a7fc-832f779a1817.bibliography: Petersen, Andrew, et al., *The Medieval and Ottoman Hajj Route in Jordan: An Archaeological and Historical Study*, Oxford: Oxbow Books, 2012.
keywords: Hijaz Railway; Hajj; pilgrimage; passenger carriage; Mecca; Medina; Jerusalem

d7e2a6e6-e1c7-57b6-a8e7-ae3661622194.name: Photograph of the Mahmal ceremony
d7e2a6e6-e1c7-57b6-a8e7-ae3661622194.short_description: This photograph shows the Mahmal preparing to leave Cairo for Mecca. It is has the title: '*Le Mahmal no 140*' with the signature of Abdullah Freres. Abdullah Frères were three Ottoman Armenian brothers who ran photographic studios in Istanbul, Cairo and Izmir. In 1862 they were named official royal photographers to the Ottoman court with the entitlement to use the royal monogram. Their studio operated between 1858-99 and while they were appointed to photograph Sultan Abdülaziz and Sultan Abdülhamid II, they were also commissioned to document aspects of the Ottoman Empire. This image was also reproduced on postcards and was also used in Saleh Soubhy’s *Pèlerinage à la Mecque et à Médine*. Visible on the mahmal is the date 1304 (AH), with part of the name of the Khedive Muhammd Tawfiq, meaning that the Mahmal was sent by order of Sultan Abdülhamid II.
