d7ef6db7-d420-5a6c-aea4-887924e0ab65.name: Hammam al-Samara
d7ef6db7-d420-5a6c-aea4-887924e0ab65.description:
The Hammam al-Samara is one of six antique hammams that served Gaza’s inhabitants and visitors. According to the foundation inscription, it dates back to the Mamluk period. Built of well-cut stone, its floor drops 3 m. below street level. Like all public hammams, it also served social functions.  
  
An inscription inside the hammam records a restoration attributed to the Mamluk governor Sanjar ibn Abdullah around 1320 AD. The hammam consists of three main sections: the reception hall, the bathing hall and a general utilities area. Its entrance door is situated on the northern wall towards the city centre. A vaulted corridor leads into the square reception hall, the floor of which is paved with coloured and geometrically designed pieces of marble. An octagonal fountain, covered by a dome, is found in the centre. Two iwans surround the reception hall from the east and south; this is where people sit and change their clothes. This hall leads to the bathing room through a middle hall. The hammam itself is covered with coloured marble tiles, and heated by the hot-air system that passes underneath the floor.

d9e955c1-2a6e-5af6-be73-7eb332bb3d48.name: Ausbootung in Haifa. (Disembarking in Haifa)
d9e955c1-2a6e-5af6-be73-7eb332bb3d48.description: The photograph shows Haifa’s waterfront railway facilities. A passenger train stands directly beside the stone quay, while a large crowd gathers between the railway carriages and the water and on a boat. Thousands of pilgrims and travellers travelled through Haifa, arriving at the port and continuing by rail through Daraa toward the Hijaz; some remained in the city for several days, contributing to local commercial and service activities. Haifa also developed as a gateway for international tourism and some offices organised railway trips from Haifa through Samakh and the Sea of Galilee toward Damascus.

dbb56934-3455-538f-8cb8-10ecee31b70c.name: Map of the Hamidiye Hejaz Railway under construction
dbb56934-3455-538f-8cb8-10ecee31b70c.description: This rare official map of the Hejaz Railway, issued in 1903 during its construction from Damascus to Medina, reflects the Ottoman Empire's ambition to enhance trade and facilitate pilgrimage. Supervised by chief engineer Hadji Mukhtar Bey, the map details field surveys and the planned railway network, covering areas from northern Syria to south of Mecca. It distinguishes between completed and projected sections, highlights proposed extensions to Mecca and Jeddah, and marks major roads and caravan routes, capturing the early stages of the railway's development before its completion in 1908.

dc22fbbb-3a0b-58bb-82f9-7523c4e9d4d5.name: Official Hijaz Railway postcards
dc22fbbb-3a0b-58bb-82f9-7523c4e9d4d5.short_description: In 1900 the Ottoman Sultan Abdülhamid II (r.1876–1909) began the construction of a railway line connecting Damascus to the holy cities of Medina and Mecca. Built by public subscription and with an appeal to Muslims of the world for financial support, the railway line began from Damascus and reached Medina in 1908, never reaching Mecca. The financing for the Hijaz Railway was initially meant to come entirely from charitable donations and in May 1900 Sultan Abdülhamid II began the process with a sizeable donation from his personal funds. Despite national and foreign generosity towards the donations campaign, it soon became clear that this alone was insufficient to raise the funds needed for the construction. Therefore, the government sought to raise funds in many other ways, including the commission of postcards amongst other German-made products, in order to generate further yield. With the title ‘*Vue du chemin-de-fer Hamidié de Hedjaz*’ and with labels in French and Turkish, the postcards depict the construction of the Railway as well as general views and inauguration celebrations. These were available for purchase at local post offices.

dd5bbbcb-30cc-5383-b362-bb72392b0cce.name: Nasser and the Nationalisation of the Canal
dd5bbbcb-30cc-5383-b362-bb72392b0cce.description: Hamed Owais’s Nasser and the Nationalisation of the Canal can be used to discuss the Cold War period and the rise of twentieth-century Arab nationalism. Painted in 1957, the work refers to Gamal Abdel Nasser’s nationalisation of the Suez Canal in 1956, a moment that became a powerful symbol of anti-imperialism, national sovereignty, and Arab political self-confidence. Owais presents Nasser as a heroic leader surrounded by the people, transforming a specific political event into an image of collective hope and revolutionary legitimacy. The painting is especially useful for explaining how art participated in the construction of Nasserist ideology, where modernisation, social justice, and independence from British and French control were visually linked to the figure of the leader. At the same time, the work opens a discussion about the double nature of political development in the Middle East: the promise of liberation and national dignity on one side, and the centralisation of power around a charismatic state authority on the other.

dd7c1d21-573b-5dd3-8f6f-94141d1320e3.name: Safi ibn Vali’s Anis al-Hujjaj (‘Pilgrims’ Companion’)
dd7c1d21-573b-5dd3-8f6f-94141d1320e3.short_description:
Written during the year-long pilgrimage undertaken by the author, Safi ibn Vali, in 1676–77, the Anis al-Hujjaj (‘Pilgrims’ Companion’) gives advice to prospective pilgrims on every aspect of the journey: which ships to choose, how to stay healthy, the places to visit, the rituals to be observed and the people one is likely to encounter. Safi ibn Vali’s own pilgrimage (he commenced his journey on 12 Rajab 1087/ 20 September 1676) was made possible through the financial help of Zib al-Nisa, a daughter of the Mughal emperor Awrangzeb, for whom he had written a commentary on the Qur’an.  
  
This manuscript belongs to a long-established tradition of guides to the Holy Places (see MSS 1038), although the illustrations here differ in that they combine the diagrammatic views normally found in such guides with vivid and colourful scenes of the pilgrims and their caravans. The illustrations are simple in their conception yet their attention to detail is acute. They provide a cogent picture of camp life of pilgrims in the late 17th century.  
  
The illustrations:  
  
View of the port of Surat and the ships carrying pilgrims (folio 2b). Surat, on the Western coast of India, north of Bombay, was one of the main points of departure to Arabia. The view is oriented to the south.  
The pilgrims’ ships crossing the Sea of Oman (folio 3b). The two larger ships carry pilgrims; one, on the right, appears to be casting (or raising) anchor. The smaller vessels may be fishing boats.  
The mish‘ar al-haram and the ritual of collecting pebbles (folio 10a). The painting shows the pilgrims in the region of Muzdalifa, in a state of ihram (ritual purity), collecting pebbles.  
The pilgrims in the town of Mina, being shaved, making sacrifices and casting pebbles at the Devil (folio 10b). This day corresponds to ‘Id al-Adha on 10 dhu’l-Hijjah, the feast commemorating the Sacrifice of Abraham. By this stage, the pilgrims, who are in a full state of ihram indicated by their white garments, have already completed their initial circumambulation of the Ka‘bah (the welcome tawaf); the ritual of running between the hills of Safa and Marwa (sa‘iyy) recalling Hagar’s desperate search for water for her son Isma‘il; the day of prayer at ‘Arafat – a most holy time when every pilgrim stands alone with God; and the gathering of pebbles at Muzdalifa in preparation for the stoning of the Devil at Mina. This recalls yet another chapter in the Abrahamic narrative in which Isma‘il stones the Devil seven times (the ritual is illustrated in the upper right-hand corner of the painting). After this a sacrifice is made. The pilgrims are released from most of the restrictions imposed by the state of ihram; men shave their heads and beards; women have their hair clipped. Pilgrims can now wear their normal clothes and leave for Mecca, where they perform another essential rite, a further circumambulation of the Ka‘bah known as the tawaf al-ifadah, which takes place on the same day.  
The birthplaces of the Prophet Muhammad; Fatimah; Abu Bak al-Siddiq; as well as the Madrasah of Sultan Sulayman, and a Bektashi lodge (folio 11b). These are shrines to visit in the vicinity of Mecca, which are not part of the hajj rituals.  
Plan of the Masjid al-Haram in Mecca with the Ka‘bah (folio 12a).  
The camp of North African caravan of pilgrims (folio 15a).  
The camp of Egyptian caravan of pilgrims (folio 15b).  
The camp of the Syrian caravan of pilgrims (folio 16a). Unlike the pilgrims from North Africa and Egypt, the Syrian pilgrims are richly dressed and carry swords and gold daggers. Ahmad Pasha, the Syrian Amir al-Hajj, is identified by a caption (top left).  
The camp of the desert Arabs and the people of Najd (folio 16b).  
The camp of the caravans of the Indian (top) and Iranian pilgrims (folio 17a).  
Officials, scribes and secretaries (folio 17b). This is a small illustration, which is not captioned.  
Sharif Barakat, hakim haramayn sharifayn (‘Governor of the two Holy Sanctuaries’), riding to meet the envoy of Sultan Mehmed \[IV\], the Emperor of Rum (folio 18a).  
‘Abdi Pasha, the Amir al-Hajj of the Egyptian caravan, on his way from Mecca to Medina (folio 18b).  
The port of Mucha, in the Yemen (folio 21a). The illustration shows the pilgrims’ ships departing from the port as well as Sayyid Husayn, the Governor of Mucha, riding his horse (bottom right).  
The port of Jeddah (folio 22b). This view is very similar to that of Mucha (folio 21a) in that it combines views of the city and the pilgrims’ ships with one of the Governor of the city, Sunjuq.  
Man attacked by a lion (folio 21b); Man saved from the jaws of a lion (folio 23a); A feast (folio 23b). The three small-scale paintings are illustrations to a parable about a very poor woman taking pity on some beggars passing by and feeding them; her act of generosity was rewarded when a stranger saved her son from being eaten by a lion. The feast is probably in celebration of the son’s safe return to his mother.

dda1f156-078a-5c9d-8e0c-b4292f3ca0b4.name: Advertisement for organised trips from Cairo to Medina
dda1f156-078a-5c9d-8e0c-b4292f3ca0b4.description: Naturally, the Hijaz Railway was not only used during the Hajj season but was also employed on other religious occasions. For instance, a poster advertising a package ship-and-train journey on AH 16 Rabaj 1332 / AD 15 June 1914 from Alexandria to Medina via Haifa, where the travellers would change over to the railway, celebrates the occasion of the *Mi‘raj* (the Prophet’s Night Ascension) on 27 Rajab. The visit was arranged by the Austro-Hungarian shipping company Österreichischer Lloyd in conjunction with the Hijaz Railway Company. Österreichischer Lloyd was formed in AH 1249 / AD 1833, Trieste and by AH 1303 / AD 1886 was one of the biggest shipping companies in the world. The company had a long-standing presence in Egypt and until AH 1322 / AD 1914 Lloyd boats were the quickest and steadiest link between Europe and Egypt. It stands to reason therefore that the company would work in tandem with the railway service to create a package trip for travel to Medina.

ddd75581-2e37-5baa-8483-63c54f368af5.name: Dress
ddd75581-2e37-5baa-8483-63c54f368af5.short_description: Long black silk dress (*malas*), narrow at the waist, wide at the bottom, embroidered with cross-stitch dark blue and red on the chest and on the front side, worn by women of the al-Druze tribes, with a shirt underneath. This object illustrates the variegated composition and the demographic changes of the Jordan population in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It also shows how the different populations brought with them their fashion, costumes and rites which contributed to the multifaceted social and cultural heritage of Jordan. The al-Druze tribes migrated from Syria (Hawran) to northeast Jordan in the early twentieth century because of their support for the Syrian revolution against the French occupation.

de79e1c8-f7fb-5e5c-8cba-6385718388c1.name: One Su‘udi Riyal
de79e1c8-f7fb-5e5c-8cba-6385718388c1.description: This silver riyal was struck at Mecca in 1348 AH (1929–30) by Abd al-Aziz ibn Saud, who had completed his conquest of the Hijaz in 1925 and at the time styled himself King of the Hijaz, Najd and its Dependencies. Unlike the purely calligraphic coinage of Sharif Hussein, it combines inscriptions with palm trees and crossed swords, motifs that anticipate the later emblem of Saudi Arabia. Its inscription names Mecca as the place of minting. The coin belongs to the brief years between the end of Hashemite rule in the Hijaz and the proclamation of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 1932.

e0f05556-5282-5134-9488-cb1139890651.name: 'Jerusalem Railway Station. 325. La Gare'
e0f05556-5282-5134-9488-cb1139890651.description: This is a cropped albumen print made from an original negative by the American Colony. It may be the same as the picture No. 28 on page 2 in "1911 Revised and Enlarged Catalogue of Lantern Slides made by the American Colony, Jerusalem..." (published by Vester & Co., Jerusalem). The picture shows the Baldwin locomotive No. 3  on the right with "Ramleh" on a plaque on its side. On the left are three carriages, one with the letters "J.J" (i.e. the Jaffa-Jerusalem line) on its side. The Jerusalem train station building can be seen behind the carriages, with a pole on its roof for a flag. Three engineers and one local man can be seen in the picture."American Colony, Jerusalem" appears in the lower right-hand corner. The letter "s" in Jerusalem is inverted. Similar inverted letters appeared in another American Colony print (see P 1734). In a band at the bottom of the print: "Jerusalem Railway Station 325 La Gare". A partly scratched out plate number "18" or 1S" appears in the lower left-hand corner.

e1be7517-b6b1-576b-8acd-653f24c29ba9.name: *Hijaz Railway Station, Damascus*
e1be7517-b6b1-576b-8acd-653f24c29ba9.short_description: The Hijaz station was originally built in 1903 to provide faster transportation for Pilgrims to Medina. So the today closed-down railway station used to be an essential transport and communication link. Furthermore it was built to integrate aloof provinces better into the Ottoman state and hence establish a closer political and economic connection. The new building completed in 1917 also embodies a desire for innovation in terms of design: its architecture is a mix between traditional local Ottoman elements and monumentalizing features of historicism.

e2bed9ed-caa1-5725-83f6-d3e744776900.name: Our Epic Tale
e2bed9ed-caa1-5725-83f6-d3e744776900.description: Jassim Al Zaini’s Our Epic Tale can be used to discuss regional development, cultural memory, and the construction of modern identity in the Gulf. Although the work emerges from a Qatari context, it also speaks to broader transformations across the region during the oil era, when societies were redefining their future while preserving links to local traditions. The figures’ traditional clothing suggests that development is not presented as something imposed from outside, but as a process rooted in local people, customs, and collective memory. In this sense, the painting can be read as a visual statement, almost a political manifesto, in which modernisation is linked to cultural continuity rather than cultural replacement. The work is also useful for discussing how Gulf modern art participated in shaping narratives of progress, identity, and locally grounded development.

e422469d-7ceb-50c4-964a-04003f9d8360.name: A commemorative coin
e422469d-7ceb-50c4-964a-04003f9d8360.description: Such is the enduring interest and pride in the old Ottoman railway that it has inspired a wide and varied stream of commemorative issues and mementos, both from within the Arab world and beyond. Articles still regularly appear in railway magazines and historical journals, with modern and archive images to illustrate the text. In the years following the inauguration of the railway, numerous postcards were printed in Ottoman Turkish and French, displaying all aspects of the line, its landscape, buildings and rolling stock. The railway has been celebrated by the issue of items as diverse as cigarette cards and advertisements for French chocolatiers and in recent years there have been commemorative issues of coins and stamps in Turkey, Syria and Jordan.

e4bbe6bf-da24-5343-a888-89a40958c64c.name: Plan and view of the Holy Sanctuary at Mecca, published by Thomas Tegg, London 1825
e4bbe6bf-da24-5343-a888-89a40958c64c.short_description: This plate is from George Sale’s translation of the Qur’an. This edition of Sale’s work was published in a two-volume work in 1825, by Thomas Tegg without the Preliminary Discourse or the Memoir of the Translator, which makes up a large part of Sale’s original translation of 1734. The 1734 edition was known to be the first English translation of the Qur’an from the original Arabic. This plate is the same as that in the 1734 edition, and consists of two depictions: ‘*Plan of the Temple of Mecca*’ and ‘*View of the Temple of Mecca*’. It has a key to the significant parts of the Haram and a note stating that the references on both the plan and the view show the same locations. This plan however is missing the signature of the original engraver A.Motte. Hand colour tinting is commonly seen in Tegg’s publishing, however it is rare to find this particular plate from Sale’s *Koran* detached and so finely coloured. It may have been removed, coloured and used as artwork in its own right.

e67f38ec-fa2d-5d97-b5a7-c6d7c6f6bd23.name: Aqsa Mosque.
e67f38ec-fa2d-5d97-b5a7-c6d7c6f6bd23.description:
The Aqsa Mosque is a rectangular building within the Haram al-Sharif. The Haram site slopes from the north to the south and this tendency is addressed by a platform that traverses it, and upon which the mosque was erected. The layout of the present mosque is the result of reconstructions and modifications that have characterised a number of building stages in different periods, and which are the subject of some debate among historians and researchers.  
The first stages of construction of the Aqsa Mosque are associated with the Caliph 'Umar bin al-Khattab (r. AH 13–23 / AD 634–44) who erected a *mihrab* and a simple mosque on the same site as the present mosque. Mujir al-Din (d. AH 928 / AD 1521), an historian and authority on the architecture of Jerusalem, mentions that Caliph 'Umar while clearing the Haram area of debris, uncovered the sacred rock. He consulted those with him about the ideal position of the mosque and was advised to situate it to the north of the rock, but he refused, saying: “But we must make its *qibla*, its front \[any part of the wall on the south\], as has the Prophet of God made the *qibla* of our mosques, their front”. In about AH 49–50 / AD 670, the famous traveller Arculf stated that the mosque was located in the southern area of the Haram; it was erected on great wooden piers constructed from re-used material found in the region and that the mosque was widened to accommodate 3000 worshippers.  
Nothing tangible remains of the original mosque, known as the Masjid al-'Umari, since it was renovated at the beginning of AH 65 / AD 685.  
The Aqsa Mosque was built during the reign of Abd al-Malik. It had 15 arcades, none of which have survived intact except those on the southern wall, due to the fact that the mosque was badly damaged by a number of earthquakes and was restored a number of times.  
During the Crusader period the Aqsa Mosque was converted into a church. A large recess was added in the eastern side, corresponding to the layout of churches facing the east. The recess remains to this day.  
The present al-Aqsa mosque has nine entrances: seven of them are located in the northern wall, one in the west wall and another in the east. The northern wall is preceded by a colonnade composed of seven slabs of stone, each covered by an intersecting vault. The colonnade opens out on to the plaza of the Haram al-Sharif through a large tapered arch.  
The ground plan of the mosque is a rectangle measuring 50 m x 80 m. It is composed of seven aisles extending from north to south; the middle one being the widest and highest of them. The three western colonnades are supported by large piers, while the eastern colonnades are supported by a series of marble columns imported from Italy during the restoration of this section by the High Islamic Council in the first half of the 20th century. At the southern end of the middle aisle there is a wooden semi-circular dome supported by corner squinches. Below the dome is the beautiful *mihrab* built by order of Salah al-Din Ayyubi (Saladin) when he liberated the mosque from the Franks in AH 583 / AD 1187.
e67f38ec-fa2d-5d97-b5a7-c6d7c6f6bd23.short_description: The present building is a product of many architectural developments, since all the dynasties that ruled the Islamic state left their mark on this building, which also fell victim to successive earthquakes. The last catastrophe was the result of an arson attack in 1969. Not much remains of the first building stages (Umayyad); its form has changed as a result of continuous renovation and restoration and it has been lengthened and not widened as is the case for Umayyad mosques. It is now composed of seven colonnades, the widest in the middle, and is topped by a gabled roof. It is connected to the miracle of the *Isra’* and *Mi’raj* (Night of the Prophet’s Ascension) for the site was mentioned in the Qur’an.
e67f38ec-fa2d-5d97-b5a7-c6d7c6f6bd23.method_for_datation: The building is dated by inscriptions, historical sources, as well as evidence of finds from archaeological excavations.

e7371a10-6fed-5f3b-b834-5b48379f0edf.name: Celebrations outside the station.
e7371a10-6fed-5f3b-b834-5b48379f0edf.description: The German field-postcard part of the German series Die Türkei im Weltkriege (Turkey in the World War) records the procession organised outside Damascus’s Hijaz Railway Station following the arrival of Jamal Pasha during the First World War. According to the printed caption, a military band leads cadets, military school pupils and members of the Jugendwehr, or youth corps, around the station. Their participation reflects the wartime mobilisation of education and youth to physical training and elementary military preparation. The station functions here as a ceremonial entrance to Damascus, where military authority and public spectacle took place. Beside the station stands the Izzat al Malla Building, one of the prominent structures in the developing Halbouni district adjacent to the station.

e8c3f98d-322b-5f12-ac61-73a1b189f9cc.name: Station du Chemin de fer El-Mina. Tripoli, Syrie (El-Mina Railway Station, Tripoli, Syria)
e8c3f98d-322b-5f12-ac61-73a1b189f9cc.description: El-Mina railway station at Tripoli opened in 1911, initially connecting Tripoli with Homs by a single-track gauge. The D.H.P.’s Tripoli–Homs line was approximately 102 km long. Its position at El-Mina (the port of Tripoli) provided the Syrian interior with a direct railway connection to the Mediterranean. The commercial consequences were already apparent in 1912 when British Foreign Office trade reports recorded that goods including wool, hides, liquorice root and cotton, which had previously been exported through Beirut, were increasingly passed through Tripoli after the railway opened.

e8fc4581-ee8f-583c-a11e-54b1e44bda1a.name: Arabic eye liner, *kohl* and perfume container
e8fc4581-ee8f-583c-a11e-54b1e44bda1a.short_description: Padded bag to hold three small brass bottles of Arab eye-liner, perfumes and essential oils. It was used as a wall decoration. Decorated with silk tassels, glass beads, Egyptian and Ottoman coins. The Jordanian economy relied on trades and crafts and new waves of people started to settle in the Jordanian territory for these purposes. This object is an example of how traditional fashion reflected the variegated population composition of the area in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It is also an example of local personal attire, fashion, costumes and rites.

e9356fd1-dca6-50f2-ac3e-5ca44323f2e2.name: Fairouz
e9356fd1-dca6-50f2-ac3e-5ca44323f2e2.description: In this mural in Beirut’s Gemmayze district, artist Yazan Halwani depicts Fairouz, one of Lebanon’s most revered singers and a powerful symbol of shared cultural identity. The subject was chosen in response to local residents, who associated Fairouz with memories of “the old days” of the neighbourhood. For Halwani, such figures offer an alternative to the political and sectarian symbols that have long occupied Beirut’s walls. By placing Fairouz in public space, he transforms the wall into a site of collective memory, nostalgia, and civic belonging, affirming a Lebanese cultural identity capable of crossing religious and political divisions.
keywords: Beirut; Gemmayze; Lebanon; Fairouz; Yazan Halwani; street art; mural; urban art

e952d626-e57d-5b8e-b2e2-24763b1c7b83.name: Receipt for a subscription among the Italians in Tunisia to buy Italy a plane
e952d626-e57d-5b8e-b2e2-24763b1c7b83.short_description:
We do not know whether the Italians living in Tunisia who collected money to buy Italy a plane were aware that Italy would use planes to bomb civilians in Libya. To be sure, they supported Italian expansionist policy.  
This receipt bears the signature of the treasurer of the committee that was collecting funding to buy Italy a plane, Giuseppe Di Vittorio, the owner of a successful construction company. The donor, Ugo Moreno, was another “big man” of the Italian community in Tunisia: a lawyer, he established a bank (Banca Italiana di Credito), in 1901 started an oil company (Societé du Pétrole) and in 1919 became town councillor in Tunis.
e952d626-e57d-5b8e-b2e2-24763b1c7b83.author: Massimo Sanacore

e99ae084-468e-510d-90bc-109658d66887.name: Sarma woman's dress
e99ae084-468e-510d-90bc-109658d66887.description: Example of sarma, an Ottoman metallic-thread embroidery technique, spread across the Levant during Ottoman rule as urban communities adopted and embraced the style as part of elite and festive dress. Characterised by intricate gold and silver threadwork, sarma became particularly associated with urban centres such as Jerusalem, Jaffa, and Damascus, where members of the social elite wore richly embellished garments on ceremonial and festive occasions.

e9c14343-1afd-549d-97f2-fce633b6f055.name: City Walls and Gates
e9c14343-1afd-549d-97f2-fce633b6f055.description:
Bab al-Jabiya was built by the Atabeg ruler, Nur al-Din Mahmud bin Zangi in 560/1164, re-using Roman stone blocks, and it was completed by the Ayyubid ruler, al-Malik al-Mu‘azzam, in 624/1227. The brackets of the defensive machicolations are visible from the exterior while on the interior is an Arabic inscription set in a tabula ansata (a rectangular frame with triangular edges) recording the patronage of Nur al-Din. The market, which extended out from Bab al-Jabiya, is closely related to the needs and trading activities of pilgrims and travelling merchants as it is considered to be the nearest extension of the pilgrimage route that heads southward to Mecca. Such economic activity oriented towards people passing through, as opposed to the inhabitants of the town, created order and security.  
  
Tower of Nur al-Din is located inside the courtyard of a small workshop/hotel called Funduq al-Islah and it features one of the bestpreserved inscription bands in Arabic, recording Nur al-Din’s refortification efforts of 568/1173.  
  
Bab al-Saghir Cemetery is venerated by all Muslims and it holds many important tombs, including those of the Prophet’s family, his companions and many of the city’s elite throughout the centuries. Some of the oldest existing tombstones date to the 5th/10th and 6th/11th century with distinctive floriated kufic epigraphy, testimony to the attention and restorations given to the cemetery during the Atabeg and Ayyubid period.  
  
It was rebuilt by Nur al-Din in 551/1156 on the foundations of the Roman Gate of Mars. It is the southernmost gate of the city. As the name indicates, its scale is small, more easily defensible, and it is equipped with machicolations.  
  
Bab Kisan is also based on an original Roman gate, dedicated to Saturn, its lower courses of large stone blocks still in place. It was rebuilt during the initial Arab conquests in the 1st/7th century, with remains evident inside the chapel, and again entirely refortified by Nur al-Din in 549/1154. As a city gate, Bab Kisan was again renovated by the Mamluks before it finally became incorporated into the church building.  
  
Bab Sharqi is the oldest extant standing monument in Damascus. It still preserves its original Roman form, attributed to the reign of Augustus (d. AD 14), during which it was called the Gate of the Sun, and mentioned in the Bible as the “Street Called Straight”. Bab Sharqi comprises a triple passageway, a large central arch and two flanking smaller arches. A single gate being more defensible, the two side entrances were blocked up during the Islamic period. The minaret is evidence of Nur al-Din’s reconstructions, as are the extensions of the wall, albeit with smaller stones, the arrow slits and the machicolations.  
  
The Tower of al-Salih Ayyub allocates the north-eastern corner of the city walls. It is part of the final refortification programme of the Ayyubid period under al-Salih Ayyub (d. 646/12478). Traces of the gardens that once bloomed along the northern stretches of the city wall and the Barada river are faintly echoed by the patches of greenery around the tower.  
  
Bab Touma, which was in Roman times the Gate of Venus, stands as a stately double gate, which underwent reconstruction during the Ayyubid period in 624/1227, and Mamluk defensive and decorative additions in 734/1333–4. The exceptionally well-preserved quality of this gate is exemplary. It features a guardroom and arrows slits above the arch, flanked by a pair of box machicolations.  
  
Bab al-Salam, known in the medieval period, Bab Salama – the Gate of Soundness, health and peace – it is one of the most beautiful gates of the city. There is a prominent monumental inscription on the gate’s lintel. This is a 7th-/13th-century Ayyubid reconstruction built by al-Salih Isma‘il, smoothly incorporating Roman blocks and Nur al-Din’s extensions of 561/1171–2. The attractive masonry along the arch of the gate is decorated with a pronounced ablaq motif of alternating limestone and basalt. Arrow-slits and box machicolations protrude around the corner to overlook the bend in the river as well as the communications routes beyond. Its riverside location made it a popular spot for tanneries which required water for the manufacture of leather goods.  
  
Bab al-Faradis, meaning Gate of Paradise, alludes to the once-blossoming district along the banks of the river. The structure dates from Nur al-Din’s period and it was originally constructed as a double gateway, as can be seen by the cross-vaulted ceiling in front of the gate.  
  
Bab al-Faraj, or the Gate of Deliverance, is the only gate that has no Roman precedent but is entirely the work of Nur al-Din, built in 549/1154. Located closest to the citadel, its name indicates the sense of optimism and triumph Nur al-Din was establishing in the city. This gate was also refortified by the Ayyubids and rebuilt again in the 7th/13th century.
e9c14343-1afd-549d-97f2-fce633b6f055.author: Abd al-Razzaq Moaz, Zena Takieddine
keywords: Damascus; city walls; city gates; Bab al-Jabiya; Bab al-Saghir; Bab Kisan; Nur al-Din; Syria

eaeeec58-9829-515d-bff2-68d336df3f72.name: Maqam (Sanctuary) of the Prophet David.
eaeeec58-9829-515d-bff2-68d336df3f72.description:
This complex is known in Arabic sources by the name of the Maqam (Sanctuary) of the Prophet David, although the Tomb of David is actually located on the eastern mountain slope in an area known today as David's City.  
According to Western, Christian accounts the upper hall of the complex known as 'Alliyat Suhyun (Palace of Zion) is where the Last Supper was held, while the lower level is believed to be the place where Christ washed the feet of his disciples. Thus the complex is an important holy site for Muslims, Christians and Jews alike and the history of the site, as well as the exchange of control over it by the three aforementioned religions, reflects aspects of the deep differences in opinion that encircle it.  
The development of the site began with a church known as the Small Church of God, but no sooner was it established in AD the 4th or 5th century, when another church known by the name of the Church of the Apostles was established as a memorial to the Last Supper. After that, the Small Church of God was enlarged and its name was changed to the Church of Zion, or the Mother of all Churches. In the wake of the Persian invasion of Jerusalem in AD 614, the Church of Zion was burned down and suffered great damage. In the AH 6th / AD 12th century, the Frankish Franciscans undertook the construction of a monastery on the eastern mountain slope believed to be the site of the Tomb of the Prophet David. They built a two-storey structure: the ground floor commemorating Christ washing the feet of his disciples, and the upper floor in memory of the Last Supper.  
The Muslims also took an interest in the site, and during the Ayyubid period (AH 615–16 / AD 1219) they took control of the building, adding a *mihrab* on the ground floor in the vaulted hall dedicated to the Prophet David. The Muslims continued to allow Christians to visit the upper hall.  
The Franciscans subsequently obtained some more ground on the eastern mountain slope of the Prophet David and erected a number of buildings under the aegis of the Mamluk Sultanate. At this point the Jewish community began to take an interest in the Tomb of David, developing an association with an unknown grave in the lower hall believed by the Jews to be the Tomb of the Prophet David. Thus a huge dissension grew up during the Mamluk period between a sect of the Jewish community and the Christian population. A number of Mamluk sultans tried to decide to which faith the site belonged. These differences were not limited to those residing in Jerusalem, but foreign powers also entered into the fray, making the Mamluk sultanate waver in its conclusive decision to the two opposing sides. In AH 930 / AD 1524, in order to bring the situation to a conclusion once and for all, Sultan Sulayman the Magnificent expelled the Franciscan Brotherhood from the site and transformed it into a mosque and an Islamic site. Ever since that time until the year 1948, when it came under Israeli control, the site remained in Muslim control and in the continual custody of the Dajani family.  
The *maqam* is a large architectural complex, composed of a number of buildings and courtyards, a large part of which are used presently as a Jewish religious school. The complex has three entrances, and contains three open courtyards and three mosques. The mosque erected in the lower level was transformed into a synagogue, while the second mosque is the hall which was formerly dedicated to the Last Supper. The third mosque is closed.
eaeeec58-9829-515d-bff2-68d336df3f72.short_description: Christians believed that this was the site of the Last Supper. Muslims have demarcated it as the site of David’s *maqam* (tomb) and some Jews also accept this identification. A church was built on the site in the Byzantine period and Frankish Franciscans built a monastery on it. The Ayyubids added a *mihrab* and transformed part of the complex into a mosque. The Ottomans then added a *zawiya* and turned it over into the hands of a Jerusalemite family, al-Dajani. In 1948 the site came under Jewish control and it was transformed into synagogues and religious schools.
eaeeec58-9829-515d-bff2-68d336df3f72.method_for_datation: The building is dated by an inscription on the entrance to the hall dedicated to the Last Supper, and by historical information according to the accounts of historians interested in Jerusalem. Mamluk documents that were published by the historian Ahmad Darraj in 1968 also lent credence to the date.

f0667100-6159-569b-9a0e-84fec1b968f0.name: Headdress
f0667100-6159-569b-9a0e-84fec1b968f0.short_description: Three bands of silver chain fitted around the sides and over the crown of the head and attached to a surrounding fabric patterned in minute beadwork and sewn with various Ottoman and Russian coins. From this head-piece hangs a long piece of cotton sewn with coins of the Ottoman Empire with a rectangular pendant and multiple red and green silk tassels on the back. Headdresses like this one were worn by married women, as silver was the most common jewellery. The dowry of silver and gold jewellery was given by the groom to the bride. The Ottoman and Russian coins reflect the social and economic situation of Jordan between the end of the 19th century and the early 20th century, when it was part of the Ottoman empire and it was influenced by population movements, demographic changes and trade with distant countries.

f0e2d598-8e69-5768-bd25-d9db967e1292.description: According to a plaque below the images, the painting depicts the pilgrimage of ‘Abbas Hilmi II, the Khedive of Egypt, which he performed in 1909. His portrait is on the left; on the right is that of Mehmed V Rashad, the contemporary Ottoman sultan. To the left and right of the Ka‘bah, which occupies the centre of the painting, are depictions of the Mosque of the Prophet in Medina and the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem. Many of the remaining images are based on photographs of the hajj published in the July 1953 issue of National Geographic.

f243ea50-61a0-52e5-843b-6c277186a513.name: Caiffa (Palestine), Date de l´installation du Chemin de fer du Hedjaz. Memorial Monument (The Exalted Column Memorial Monument, the beginning of the construction of the Hijaz Railway, Haifa, Palestine)
f243ea50-61a0-52e5-843b-6c277186a513.description: The Exalted Column, Haifa, known in Ottoman Turkish as Sütūn-u ʿĀlī and in Arabic as al-’Amud al-’Ali (العمود العالي), is a monument erected in 1903 to commemorate the beginning of construction of the Haifa–Dar’a railway branch, part of the Hijaz Railway project. The monument is generally attributed to Raimondo D’Aronco, the Italian architect who served the Ottoman court during the reign of Sultan Abdülhamid II. Haifa’s location offered significant advantages over the nearby port of Acre. Connecting the railway to Haifa enabled construction materials, coal, machinery and other supplies to be delivered by sea and transported inland. It also created a transport corridor through which agricultural produce and commercial goods from inland Syria and Palestine could reach the Mediterranean coast.

f32db4ad-178e-583f-be68-731a20b86a1a.description: The map is part of the Pocket Atlas of the Ottoman Lands: The Geographical and Statistical Conditions of the Ottoman State. It represents territories extending from Egypt and the eastern Mediterranean in the west to the Euphrates River in the east, and from Damascus in the north to the Hijaz region in the south. The map identifies regions, towns, ports, deserts, mountain ranges and maritime routes in Ottoman Turkish written in Arabic script. A route beginning in Damascus and continuing through Darʿa and Maʿan toward Medina corresponds to the Hijaz Railway. The map table heading is given first in Ottoman Turkish and immediately below in Arabic, reading: "Map of the Hijaz Railway", with a list of stations underneath. Each location is accompanied by a numerical value expressed in kilometres, indicating cumulative distances measured from Damascus.

f51a4a5c-7bc4-5e4a-88be-a3cbce890510.name: Beit Nizam
f51a4a5c-7bc4-5e4a-88be-a3cbce890510.description:
Beit Nizam is located in the Maazanat al-Shahm quarter of Old Damascus. An inscription dated AH 1172 (1758–59 AD) provides evidence of its eighteenth-century history. The residence developed through successive architectural phases, with its elaborate interiors reflecting the changing artistic tastes of wealthy Damascene households during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The complex is organised around three courtyards. The fountain and walls of the first reception hall include busily colourful paintings, carving, and gilding. Sparkling brilliantly to this day is the so-called 'Qa'at al-'Inab' ('Hall of Grapes'), which represents a masterpiece of wealth and style. The extravagant use of gilded applications and mirrors reveals a very heavy European Baroque influence. One of the many ceiling mirrors shows the influence of European Baroque with its outward radiance. The Crescent and Star motifs are symbols of the Ottoman Empire and are thus evidence of the marriage between imperial and European taste in this Damascene house incorporated into established local architectural traditions.  
  
The house witnessed significant changes in Damascus during the nineteenth century, including the period of Ibrahim Pasha's rule (1832–1840). It also served as the seat of the British Consulate until 1883. According to the historical account, the residence was subsequently occupied by the al-Quwaydi family until 1926, followed by the al-Qabbani and al-Abbas families. It eventually became associated with the Nizam family, its last private occupants during the first half of the twentieth century, from whom the house acquired its present name after the family undertook renovations to the property. It was acquired by Damascus Municipality in 1974; it underwent restoration between 1987 and 1994 and was subsequently opened to visitors. Further conservation work was initiated by the Aga Khan Trust for Culture in 2008, contributing to the preservation of its historic architectural fabric and decorative interiors.

f54a1f1a-89eb-53ec-92f4-4b04e01290a2.name: Street Language
f54a1f1a-89eb-53ec-92f4-4b04e01290a2.description: Faraj Daham’s Street Language (2011) can be used to address the social dimension of Doha’s rapid urban transformation by foregrounding the construction workers who made this development physically possible. The dominant yellow and orange tones evoke Qatar’s intense climate, while the workers’ covered faces and direct gaze draw attention to issues of labour, migration, visibility, and anonymity. Rather than presenting modernisation only through architecture and urban growth, the work invites viewers to consider the human bodies behind these processes. For this reason, Street Language is especially useful for discussing Gulf modernity as a social, economic, and human phenomenon, not merely as a visual narrative of progress.

f562fef5-27de-5b9d-af36-fde217967898.name: Station de chemin de fer du port de Beyrouth (Beirut Railway Station)
f562fef5-27de-5b9d-af36-fde217967898.description: Beirut Port Train Station was established in 1903 when the railway infrastructure of Beirut was extended to reach the harbour docks during the expansion of the D.H.P. network. The port station was created to facilitate the transfer of goods arriving by sea into the railway system. This connection formed part of a wider phase of railway expansion following the renewal of the company’s concession in 1887. Construction in Rayak began in 1902 and then reached Hama. In 1903, Beirut Station was connected directly with the Beirut quay through this station. The project subsequently extended the network from the Mediterranean to the interior by the Hama–Aleppo and Homs–Tripoli branches between 1905 and 1911.

fd051a6c-6d76-5872-b5f1-48712d9ee72b.name: ‘Eye of envy’ amulet.
fd051a6c-6d76-5872-b5f1-48712d9ee72b.description:
A blue 'eye of envy' made of a moulded, blue glass disc decorated with a series of diminishing circles of yellow, then white, with a black spot at the centre. Probably a bead from a string of other similar beads, it has a hole though the side for threading. This type of glass 'eye' might also have been sewn on to garments and headdresses.  
  
Within Islamic popular belief blue eyes are thought to be envious eyes; the eye of envy is worn to repel such negative power by reflecting back to the perpetrator their own envy, thereby protecting the wearer from the effects of jealousy, thought to cause illness or disaster.  
  
Such eyes can be crudely made like this bead, or can be drawn with accuracy and quality of craftsmanship, as found in jewellery made of gold or silver; the quality does not affect the protective power. Plain blue beads are also thought to play a similar protective role, and are sometimes used in place of an eye of envy.
fd051a6c-6d76-5872-b5f1-48712d9ee72b.short_description: In popular Middle Eastern Islamic belief blue eyes are thought to be both envious and to have the ability to repel envy. This blue glass eye is worn to protect the bearer from the effects of jealousy, which may cause the loss of what is being envied or illness or disaster.

fe87deef-c455-5755-9f18-175550fef06e.name: Opening of the bridge over the Kishon (Qishon) River in the Jezreel Valley (?). A train festooned with Ottoman flags and carrying many pasengers is on the bridge, and dignitaries stand on the track.
fe87deef-c455-5755-9f18-175550fef06e.description: The photograph records an opening ceremony at a railway bridge, tentatively identified as a crossing of the Kishon River, also known as Nahr al-Muqatta‘, in the Jezreel Valley. A train decorated with Ottoman flags and carrying numerous passengers stands on the bridge, while dignitaries gather on the track. Conder and Kitchener described the Kishon as Palestine’s most important river after the Jordan, tracing a course of approximately 23 miles (37 km) from its spring-head west of Mount Tabor to the sea. Their survey records a width of approximately ten yards (9 m) and a depth of four feet (1.2 m) east of Tell el-Kassis in June 1875. Marshy ground and steep banks made crossings difficult along parts of its course, providing geographical context for the construction of railway bridges.
fe87deef-c455-5755-9f18-175550fef06e.bibliography: -Conder. C.R., Kitchener. R.E., ed. Palmer. E. H., Besant. W., The Survey of the Western Palestine Memories Of The Topography, Orography, Hydrography, and Archaeology. Vol. (L), Sheets (VI) for The Committee Of The Palestine Exploration Fund, London (1881)

fec8780a-ff2e-551c-aafa-af473f5f2afe.name: Untitled
fec8780a-ff2e-551c-aafa-af473f5f2afe.description: This work by Abdullah Hamas, a Palestinian painter, expresses the urban interconnectedness between the holy cities of Jerusalem, Medina and Mecca. By tying these sacred geographies together along a diagonal axis, Hamas recreates the intertwined  nature of those holy cities and the movement between them as expressed in the original purpose of the Hijaz Railway. The axis, in this sense, reconstitutes a new imagined railway connected centres  of urban sacrality in the Hijaz and Levant.
